en: The Mahāyāna Abhidharma-samuccaya, Fascicle One.
Composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
The *pūrvakalpa* and the *viniścaya*, each of which has four types;
the three factors that should be subsumed: the truths, the dharmas, attainments, and the treatises (*śāstra*).
How many causes for grasping signs, their establishment, and their sequence.
The detailed analysis through meaning and analogy, and the summary verse, should be understood as follows:
How many are there for each of the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and bases (āyatana)?

There are five aggregates: namely, the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha), the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha), the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha), the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha), and the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha).

There are eighteen elements (dhātus), namely: the eye element, the form element, and the eye-consciousness element; the ear element, the sound element, and the ear-consciousness element; the nose element, the odor element, and the nose-consciousness element; the tongue element, the taste element, and the tongue-consciousness element; the body element, the tangible object element, and the body-consciousness element; and the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element.

There are twelve bases (āyatana), namely: the eye-base and the form-base; the ear-base and the sound-base; the nose-base and the odor-base; the tongue-base and the taste-base; the body-base and the tangible-base; and the mind-base and the mental-object-base.

For what reason are there only five aggregates? It is to manifest the five kinds of objects pertaining to the self (*ātman*): namely, the object of the self as body and possession; the object of the self as experience; the object of the self as speech; the object of the self as the agent of all that is dharma and non-dharma; and the object of the self as the essential nature (*svabhāva*) which is the basis for those [others].
For what reason are there only eighteen elements (*dhātu*)?
Because the body, its faculties, and so forth, are able to maintain the nature of experiencing the six types of activity [of consciousness] in the past and present.
For what reason are there only twelve bases (*āyatana*)?
Because the physical body alone serves as the gateway for the growth and development of the six modes of experience in the future,
why are they called the "appropriation aggregates" (upādānaskandha)?
They are called appropriation aggregates because they are conjoined with appropriation.
What is grasping (*upādāna*)?
It refers to all desire and lust (*chandarāga*) within the aggregates (*skandha*).
For what reason is desire and lust called "grasping"?

It is called "clinging" (*upādāna*) because it draws forth and does not relinquish the aggregates (*skandha*) of the future and present; it is the longing for the future and the attachment to the present through sensual desire.
For what reason are the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*) termed "phenomena associated with clinging" (*sopādānīya-dharma*)?
It should be explained in the same manner as the aggregates (*skandha*). What is the characteristic of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*)?
The characteristic of manifesting transformation is the characteristic of form.
This is of two kinds:
first, transformation through contact; second, manifestation according to spatial direction.
What is meant by "transformation through contact"?

That is to say, when touched or confronted by hands, feet, clods of earth, stones, swords, staves, cold, heat, hunger, thirst, mosquitoes, gadflies, snakes, or scorpions, it immediately undergoes transformation and decay.
What is meant by "manifesting according to location"?
That is to say, it is manifested through spatial characteristics as such-and-such a form or this-and-that a form;
or it is produced by various mental constructions, whether by a concentrated mind or by a non-concentrated mind associated with discursive thought.
What is the characteristic of the aggregate of feeling?
Its characteristic is that of experiencing; that is to say, by means of feeling, one experiences the various maturations of the results of pure and impure karma.
What is the characteristic of the aggregate of perception?

The characteristic of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) is the characteristic of mental construction; that is to say, by means of perception, one constructs and delineates the various images and categories of phenomena, giving rise to verbal expressions according to the meanings seen, heard, sensed, and known.
What is the characteristic of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)?

Its characteristic is that of volitional activity (*abhisamskāra*). This means that by means of formations, the mind is made to act; for they drive and employ the mind within the categories of the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate.
What is the characteristic of the aggregate of consciousness?

The characteristic of discerning is the characteristic of consciousness; that is to say, by means of consciousness, one discerns various objects such as forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena.
What is the characteristic of the eye-element?

That is to say, the eye having previously or presently seen forms, as well as the ripening *ālayavijñāna* in which the seeds of this [vision] are accumulated, constitutes the characteristic of the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*).
As with the characteristic of the eye-element, so it is for the characteristics of the elements of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
What are the characteristics of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)?
They are as follows: forms that have been previously seen by the eye, and the predominance (*adhipatya*) of the eye-faculty (*cakṣurdhātu*) therein; these are the characteristics of the form realm.
As it is with the form realm, so too are the characteristics of the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibles, and mental objects (*dharmadhātu*).
What is the characteristic of the visual consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*)?

It is the discernment of forms based upon the eye and conditioned by forms, appearing as those forms; and the maturation (*vipāka*) of the *ālayavijñāna* in which the seeds of this [consciousness] are accumulated—this is the characteristic of the visual consciousness element.
Just as it is with the element of eye-consciousness, so too are the characteristics of the elements of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness.
What are the characteristics of the bases (*āyatana*)?
They should be understood in accordance with the elements, as appropriate.
How is the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) established?
It refers to all that is form, whether it be the four great elements (mahābhūta) or that which is derived from the four great elements.
What are the four great elements?
They are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element.
What is the earth element?
It is the quality of solidity and hardness.
What is the water element?
It is the nature of flowing and moisture.
What is the fire element?
It refers to the nature of warmth and heat.
What is the wind element?
It refers to the nature of lightness and mobility.
What is derived matter?

It refers to the eye faculty, the ear faculty, the nose faculty, the tongue faculty, and the body faculty; a portion of visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles; and the matter included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
What is the eye faculty?
It is the translucent matter derived from the four great elements that serves as the basis for visual consciousness.
What is the ear faculty?
It refers to the translucent matter derived from the four great elements that serves as the basis for ear-consciousness.
What is the nose faculty?
It refers to the translucent matter derived from the four great elements that serves as the basis for nose-consciousness.
What is the tongue faculty?
It is the translucent matter derived from the four great elements that serves as the basis for tongue-consciousness.
What is the body faculty?

It refers to the translucent matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) that serves as the basis for body-consciousness (*kāya-vijñāna*), which is itself derived from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). What is this matter?

It refers to the objects of the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), which is itself derived from the four great elements; namely: blue, yellow, red, white, long, short, square, round, coarse, fine, high, low, even, uneven, light, shadow, brightness, darkness, clouds, smoke, dust, mist, the color of distant space, manifesting color, and the color of the uniform expanse of space.
This, moreover, is of three kinds: namely, agreeable, disagreeable, and that which is neither. What is sound?

It is the object apprehended by the auditory faculty, produced from the four great elements; it may be agreeable, disagreeable, or neither; it may have appropriated great elements as its cause, unappropriated great elements as its cause, or both as its cause; it may be what is commonly established in the world, what is derived from [mental] formation, or what is arisen from conceptual construction; and it may be included within noble speech or not included within noble speech.
What is odor?

It refers to the object apprehended by the olfactory faculty, which is derived from the four great elements; namely, pleasant odors, unpleasant odors, neutral odors, innate odors, blended odors, and transformed odors.
What is taste?

It refers to the objects apprehended by the tongue faculty, which is itself derived from the four great elements. These are: bitter, sour, sweet, pungent, salty, and bland; or those that are agreeable, disagreeable, or both; or those that are innate, composite, or transformed.
What is the portion of the tangible?

It refers to the objects apprehended by the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), which are derived from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). These are: smoothness, roughness, lightness, heaviness, softness, slackness, tension, cold, hunger, thirst, satiety, strength, weakness, oppression, itching, stickiness, illness, old age, death, fatigue, rest, and vigor.
What is the form included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*)?

It should be known that there are five kinds: namely, extremely condensed form (*paramāṇusaṃghāta-rūpa*), extremely remote form (*dūrāntara-rūpa*), form derived from what is received (*samādāna-rūpa*), form produced by conceptual construction (*parikalpita-rūpa*), and form produced through mastery in meditative concentration (*samādhivaśitā-ja-rūpa*).
How is the aggregate of feeling established?
It refers to the six groups of feeling:
feeling born of eye-contact, feeling born of ear-contact, feeling born of nose-contact, feeling born of tongue-contact, feeling born of body-contact, and feeling born of mind-contact.
Thus, there are these six classes of feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Furthermore, there are bodily feelings that are pleasant, bodily feelings that are painful, and bodily feelings that are neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
There are pleasant mental feelings, painful mental feelings, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant mental feelings.
Furthermore, there are pleasant feelings associated with attachment, painful feelings associated with attachment, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings associated with attachment.
There is the feeling of pleasure that lacks flavor, the feeling of pain that lacks flavor, and the feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure that lacks flavor.
Furthermore, there is the feeling of pleasure based on attachment, the feeling of pain based on attachment, and the feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure based on attachment.
Pleasant feeling based on renunciation, painful feeling based on renunciation, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling based on renunciation.
What is bodily feeling?
It refers to feeling associated with the five consciousnesses.
What is mental feeling?
It refers to feeling associated with the mental consciousness.
What is feeling accompanied by attachment?
This refers to feeling associated with craving for one's own self.
What is insipid feeling?
It refers to feeling dissociated from this craving.
What is feeling based on attachment?
It refers to feeling associated with craving for the five excellent sensual pleasures.
What is feeling based on renunciation?
This refers to feeling dissociated from craving.
How is the aggregate of perception established?
It consists of the six groups of perception:

Perception born of eye-contact, perception born of ear-contact, perception born of nose-contact, perception born of tongue-contact, perception born of body-contact, and perception born of mind-contact.

By means of this perception, one may discern that which has signs, or discern that which is signless; one may discern the small, or discern the large; one may discern the immeasurable, or discern the sphere of nothingness where there is not even the slightest thing.
What is the perception of signs (*sanimitta-saṃjñā*)?
It refers to all perceptions other than those of unwholesome discourse, the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), and the attainment of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
What is the perception of signlessness (*animitta-saṃjñā*)?
This refers to all other perceptions.
What is "minor perception"?
It refers to the perception capable of cognizing the desire realm.
What is the great perception?
It refers to the perception capable of discerning the form realm.
What is the immeasurable perception?
This refers to being able to discern the perception of the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness.
What is the perception of nothingness, wherein there is nothing whatsoever?
This refers to being able to discern the perception of the sphere of nothingness.
How is the aggregate of formations established?
It refers to the six groups of volition:

volition produced by eye-contact, volition produced by ear-contact, volition produced by nose-contact, volition produced by tongue-contact, volition produced by body-contact, and volition produced by mind-contact.
Due to this volition (*cetanā*), one performs various wholesome deeds through volition, performs defilements through volition, and performs the differentiation of states through volition.

Furthermore, this very volition—excluding feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*)—together with the remaining mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) and formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), is collectively termed the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
What are the mental factors other than those [already mentioned]? They are:

attention (*manaskāra*), contact (*sparśa*), desire (*chanda*), resolve (*adhimokṣa*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), faith (*śraddhā*), shame (*hrī*), dread of blame (*apatrāpya*), non-attachment (*alobha*), non-hatred (*adveṣa*), non-delusion (*amoha*), diligence (*vīrya*), pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), non-harming (*avihiṃsā*); and attachment (*lobha*), hatred (*dveṣa*), pride (*māna*), ignorance (*avidyā*), doubt (*vicikitsā*); the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), the esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), the esteeming of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*); anger (*krodha*), enmity (*upanāha*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), vexation (*pradāsa*), envy (*īrṣyā*), avarice (*mātsarya*), deceit (*māyā*), guile (*śāṭhya*), arrogance (*mada*), harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*); lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*), lethargy (*styāna*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), laziness (*kausīdya*), heedlessness (*pramāda*), forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*), lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*), distraction (*vikṣepa*), sleep (*middha*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), applied thought (*vitarka*), and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
What is volition (*cetanā*)?

Its essence consists in the mental activity (*manas-karman*) that constructs within the mind; its function is to employ the mind with respect to the categories of the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate.
What is attention (*manasikāra*)?
It has the nature of initiating the mind and the function of maintaining the mind upon its object.
What is contact (*sparśa*)?
It has the nature of the discrimination of the transformation of the sense faculties based on the conjunction of the three, and its function is to serve as the basis for feeling (*vedanā*).
What is desire (*chanda*)?
It has as its essence the hope for the accomplishment of various desired objects; its function is to serve as the basis for right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*).
What is resolve (*adhimokṣa*)?
It has as its essence the mental retention and confirmation of a determined object according to how it was determined, and its function is to be unshakable by others.
What is mindfulness (*smṛti*)?
It has as its essence causing the mind to clearly remember and not forget an object with which one is familiar, and its function is non-distraction.
What is samādhi? Its essence is the one-pointedness of the mind upon the object of observation.
Its function is to serve as the basis for wisdom.
What is wisdom?
It has the discernment of phenomena regarding the objects of observation as its essence, and the severing of doubt as its function. What is faith?
It has as its essence the acceptance of, purification regarding, and aspiration toward that which possesses substance, virtue, and capability; its function is to serve as the basis for longing.
What is shame (*hrī*)?
It has as its essence feeling self-reproach regarding various faults and evils; its function is to serve as the basis for the cessation of unwholesome conduct.
What is shame (*hrī*)?
It has the nature of feeling bashfulness before others regarding various faults and evils; its function is as explained for *lajjā*.
What is non-attachment (*alobha*)?
Non-attachment is defined as having the essence of being unattached toward existence and the instruments of existence; its function is to serve as the basis for the non-engagement in misconduct.
What is non-hatred?

It is defined as having the essence of being free from malice toward sentient beings, their suffering, and the instruments of suffering; its function is to serve as the basis for the non-engagement in misconduct.
What is non-delusion?
It has the nature of discernment through the wisdom of retribution, scripture, and realization, and its function is to serve as the basis for the non-occurrence of unwholesome conduct.
What is diligence?

It has the nature of mental fortitude; its function is to bring the categories of wholesome qualities to completion through distinctions such as donning the armor, application, non-depression, non-retrogression, or non-satiety.
What is serenity (*praśrabdhi*)?
It has the nature of calming the heaviness and rigidity of body and mind and bringing them into a state of pliancy; its function is to eliminate all hindrances.
What is heedfulness (*apramāda*)?

It is defined as having the cultivation of all wholesome dharmas—based upon right effort and characterized by non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion—as its essence; its function is to guard the mind against all tainted (sāsrava) phenomena and to bring to fulfillment all mundane and supramundane merit.
What is equanimity (*upekṣā*)?

It is that which, based on right effort and characterized by non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion, is opposed to dwelling in affliction; its essence consists of the mind’s state of evenness, the mind’s state of rectitude, and the mind’s state of dwelling without effort; its function is to provide no basis for the persistence of afflictions.
What is non-harming (*avihiṃsā*)?
It has as its essence a portion of the wholesome root of non-aversion (*adveṣa*) characterized by compassion and pity, and its function is to refrain from injuring or afflicting others.
What is greed (*lobha*)?
It has craving for the three realms as its essence, and its function is to give rise to manifold sufferings. What is hatred?
It has mental resentment toward sentient beings, suffering, and the instruments of suffering as its essence, and its function is to serve as the basis for non-serene dwelling and unwholesome conduct.
What is pride (*māna*)?
It has as its essence the loftiness of mind based upon the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), and its function is to serve as the basis for the arising of disrespect and suffering.
What is ignorance (*avidyā*)?
This means that its essence is ignorance regarding the three realms, and its function is to serve as the basis for the arising of false certainties, doubts, and confusion among all phenomena.
What is doubt? Its essence is hesitation regarding the truths, and its function is to serve as the basis for the non-arising of wholesome qualities.
What is the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)?

It is defined as the acceptance, desire, cognition, examination, and view that, with respect to the five aggregates of clinging, regards them as "I" or "mine. Its function is to serve as the basis for all varieties of dogmatic views.
What is the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)?

It is defined as the acceptance, desire, thought, examination, and view that, in relation to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), regards them as either annihilated or eternal. Its function is to obstruct the middle way and liberation.

What is the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*)? It refers to the act of regarding various views and the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), which serve as the basis for those views, as being supreme, excellent, superior, and sublime. Its essence consists of various forms of acceptance, desire, cognition, reflection, and view; its function is to cling to that which serves as the basis for incorrect views.
What is the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)?

It refers to the body of acceptance, desire, thought, examination, and view that, in regard to various rules and observances as well as the five aggregates of grasping (*pañcopādānaskandha*) which serve as their basis, regards them as purification, liberation, and deliverance; its function is to serve as a basis for laboring without fruit.
What is wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)?

It is defined as the denial of cause, the denial of effect, the denial of function, the repudiation of existing entities, or false conceptualization. Its essence consists of various forms of acceptance, desire, awareness, reflection, and vision. Its functions are: the severing of the roots of virtue; serving as the basis for the strengthening of unwholesome roots; the arising of the unwholesome; and the non-arising of the wholesome.
Among these five views, how many are views of superimposition (*samāropa*) and how many are views of denial (*apavāda*)?

Four are views of superimposition; that is to say, they superimpose intrinsic nature and specific qualities upon the objects of knowledge, and they superimpose the status of being supreme and pure upon those very views.
Most of these are views of negation (*apavāda-dṛṣṭi*).
Regarding all views concerning the past and future limits (*pūrvānta* and *aparānta*), how many of these five views do they subsume?
It is either two or all of them.
Regarding all views concerning the indeterminate matters (*avyākṛtavastu*), how many of these five views do they subsume?
That is to say, either two or all of them.
For what fault did the Blessed One observe that he rejected the grasping at a self through five aspects regarding the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases?

This is because one observes five kinds of faults in those who embrace the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*): namely, the fault of having distinct characteristics, the fault of impermanence, the fault of lack of sovereignty, the fault of being bodiless, and the fault of attaining liberation without effort.

Regarding the five aggregates of clinging, there are twenty modes of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*): namely, reckoning form as the self, the self as possessing form, form as belonging to the self, and the self as being within form; likewise reckoning feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as the self, the self as possessing consciousness and so forth, consciousness and so forth as belonging to the self, and the self as being within consciousness and so forth.
Among these views, how many are views of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) and how many are views of what belongs to self (*ātmīyadṛṣṭi*)?
It is said that five are views of self and fifteen are views of what belongs to self.
For what reason are these fifteen [factors] considered "mine"?
Because they are associated with "mine," because they follow along with "mine," and because they are not separate from "mine.
Regarding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), should it be said that it is fully understood or not fully understood with respect to its object?
It should be said that one cannot reach a definitive resolution regarding the object, just as one falsely conceives the notion of a snake upon a rope.
What is anger (*krodha*)?

It is a portion of hatred (*dveṣa*) directed toward a presently manifest harmful appearance; its essence is mental wrath, and its function is to serve as the basis for brandishing weapons and outbursts of fury.
What is resentment (*upanāha*)?
It is defined as a portion of anger from that point onward, having the essential nature of harboring a grudge without relinquishing it, and its function is to serve as the basis for intolerance.
What is concealment (*mrakṣa*)?

It is a portion of delusion (*moha*) that, when another person correctly points out one's committed transgression, takes the form of hiding it; its function is to serve as a basis for remorse and lack of mental composure.
What is vexation (*pradāsa*)?

Having anger and resentment as its precursor, it is a portion of hatred (*dveṣa*). Its essence is the contortion of the mind; its function is to serve as the basis for arrogant, violent, and coarse speech, to give rise to non-merit (*apuṇya*), and to cause one to dwell in a state of insecurity.
What is envy (*īrṣyā*)?

It is defined as being attached to gain and profit and being unable to endure the prosperity of others; it is a derivative of hatred, having the nature of mental jealousy, and its function is to cause the mind to dwell in sorrow, distress, and lack of tranquility.
What is stinginess (*mātsarya*)?

It refers to being attached to gains and the requisites for life; it is a portion of greed, having the nature of a parsimonious mind, and its function is the failure to relinquish that which one relies upon.
What is deception?

It has as its essence the false manifestation of non-existent virtues due to attachment to gain and offerings, being a portion of greed and delusion; its function is to serve as the basis for wrong livelihood.
What is guile (*śāṭhya*)?

It has as its essence the resorting to expedient means to conceal one's actual faults and evils out of attachment to gain and offerings, being a portion of greed and delusion; its function is to obstruct correct instruction.
What is *mada* (haughtiness)?

It is defined as a portion of craving that arises based on the signs of youth, health, or long life, or upon obtaining any kind of tainted (*sāsrava*) prosperity or gain; its essence is the gladdening of the mind, and its function is to serve as the basis for all primary afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
What is harm (*vihiṃsā*)?
It is a portion of anger; its essence consists of a lack of affection, compassion, and pity, and its function is to injure and afflict sentient beings.
What is lack of shame (*āhrīkya*)?

It is defined as a portion of greed, hatred, and delusion, having the nature of not feeling shame regarding one's own faults and evils, and functioning as an associate to all primary afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
What is lack of dread (*āhrīkya*)?

It is a derivative of greed, hatred, and delusion; its essence consists in a lack of shame before others regarding various faults and evils; its function is to serve as an associate to all primary afflictions and secondary afflictions.
What is lethargy (*styāna*)?
It refers to a portion of delusion; its essence is the mind's lack of functional capacity, and its function is to obstruct vipaśyanā.
What is restlessness?
It refers to a portion of desire; its essence is the mind’s lack of tranquility due to recollecting signs of purity, and its function is to obstruct śamatha.
What is lack of faith (*aśraddhā*)?

It is a factor of delusion (*moha*), characterized by the mind’s lack of acceptance toward wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*), lack of mental purity, and lack of aspiration; its function is to serve as a basis for laziness (*kausīdya*).
What is laziness?

It is a derivative of delusion; its essence consists in attachment to sleep and reclining as a pleasure, and a lack of mental exertion; its function is to obstruct the cultivation of skillful qualities through application.
What is negligence (*pramāda*)?

Its essence consists in not cultivating wholesome dharmas due to reliance on laziness (*kausīdya*), as well as greed, hatred, and delusion; it consists in the mind’s failure to guard against tainted (*sāsrava*) dharmas. Its function is to serve as the basis for aversion to and the destruction of the wholesome.
What is forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*)?
It has as its essence mindfulness associated with the various afflictions, and its function is to serve as the basis for distraction.
What is lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*)?

It has as its essence the wisdom associated with the various afflictions; by means of this wisdom, one gives rise to improper awareness (*asamprajanya*) in the activities of body, speech, and mind, and its function is to destroy that which it relies upon.
What is distraction? It is a portion of greed, hatred, and delusion, having the nature of the mind’s dispersal.
This, moreover, is of six kinds: namely, natural distraction, external distraction, internal distraction, distraction of signs, distraction of coarse heaviness, and distraction of mental attention.
What is natural distraction?
It refers to the five groups of sensory consciousnesses.
What is external distraction?
This refers to the mind being distracted toward the five types of sensory pleasures while correctly practicing virtue.
What is internal distraction?
It refers to mental sinking, agitation, or attachment to the taste [of meditative states] while correctly practicing virtue.
What is distraction of signs?
It refers to feigning the practice of virtue in order to gain the trust and faith of others.
What is distraction of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*)?

This refers to the fact that, due to the coarse and heavy force of the grasping at "I" and "mine" and the category of the conceit of "I am," when one practices wholesome dharmas, one gives rise to the notions of "I" and "mine" as well as the conceit of "I am" toward all sensations that have already arisen, thereby grasping them with a mixture of such signs.
What is distraction of mental attention (*manasikāra-vikṣepa*)?

It refers to the scattering that occurs based on other vehicles or other meditative concentrations, whether in terms of their basis or their entry; its function is to obstruct the attainment of detachment.
What is sleep (*middha*)?

This refers to that which, depending on the causal conditions of sleep, belongs to the category of delusion; its essence is the contraction of the mind; it may be wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral; it may occur at the proper time or the improper time; it may be appropriate or inappropriate; and its function is to serve as the basis for neglecting what ought to be done.
What is remorse (*kaukṛtya*)?

It refers to that which arises based on what was done with pleasure or without pleasure, and what was done that ought to have been done or ought not to have been done. It is a derivative of delusion (*moha*), having the nature of mental regret. It may be wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral; it may occur at the proper time or the improper time; it may be appropriate or inappropriate. Its function is to obstruct the mind’s abiding in composure.
What is vitarka?
It is the mental verbalization that, based either on volition or on wisdom, seeks out [an object], having as its essence the coarse movement of the mind.
What is vicāra?
It refers to the mental verbalization that investigates either by means of volition (*cetanā*) or by means of wisdom (*prajñā*), having the nature of causing the mind to function subtly.
These two types have the function of serving as the basis for mental states that are either settled or unsettled.

Furthermore, all wholesome mental factors (*citta-saṃprayukta-dharma*) have as their function the severing of that which they oppose; the afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) have as their function the obstructing of that which can counteract them.
What are called the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*)?

These are: acquisition (*prāpti*), the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the maturation of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-vedanīya-vipāka*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the homogeneous character of a group (*nikāya-sabhāga*), birth (*jāti*), aging (*jarā*), duration (*sthiti*), impermanence (*anityatā*), the body of names (*nāma-kāya*), the body of phrases (*pada-kāya*), the body of phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*), the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), transmigration (*pravṛtti*), determination (*pratiniyama*), association (*samyoga*), rapidity (*java*), succession (*anukrama*), time (*kāla*), direction (*deśa*), number (*saṃkhyā*), and integration (*sāmagrī*).
What is "attainment"? It refers to the conventional designation of "acquisition" and "possession" regarding the increase or decrease of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena.
What is the "attainment of non-perception"?

It refers to the state where one has already abandoned desire for the Śubhakṛtsna realm but has not yet abandoned desire for the higher realms; because it is preceded by the mental attention of the perception of renunciation, the "attainment of non-perception" (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) is provisionally established with respect to the cessation of the non-continually active mind and mental factors.
What is the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)?

It refers to the designation of the attainment of cessation with respect to the cessation of all non-constant mental states and mental factors, as well as a portion of the constant mental states and mental factors, preceded by the mental attention that temporarily suspends perception, having already abandoned desire for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and transcended the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
What is the maturation of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*)?

It refers to that which is conventionally designated as the maturation of non-perception within the realm of non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*), consisting in the cessation of the non-continually active mind and mental factors.
What is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)?
It is the provisional designation for the determination of the duration of abiding, projected by prior karma within a commonality of group (*nikāyasabhāga*).
What is the commonality of group?

That is to say, for such and such sentient beings who are similar in their various types of individual existence (*ātman*), the "homogeneity of the group" (*nikāya-sabhāga*) is conventionally established. What is birth?
It is the conventional designation of "birth" for the fact that, within this homogeneity, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) which previously did not exist now come into being.
What is aging? It is the designation "aging" applied to the transformation of the continuity of conditioned phenomena within a given homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
What is duration?
That is to say, the non-disruption of the continuity of formations within a homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) is conventionally designated as "abiding.
What is impermanence?
It is the disruption of the continuity of formations within a homogeneous class that is conventionally designated as "impermanence."
What is the "name-body" (nāmakāya)?
It refers to the conventional designation of a name-body based on verbal expressions that augment the intrinsic nature of phenomena.
What is the "phrase-body" (padakāya)?
That is to say, the "phrase-group" (padakāya) is a conventional designation for the various expressions that increase the differentiation of phenomena.
What is the "syllable-group" (vyañjanakāya)?
It is the conventional designation for the various phonemes (akṣara) which serve as the basis for those two.
This is called "text" (*vyañjana*) because it is able to manifest those two [meaning and word].
It is also called "manifestation" (*vyakti*) because it is able to reveal that meaning.
Furthermore, it is called "name" (*nāman*) because it does not undergo any change.
What is the nature of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*)?
It is the non-attainment of the noble dharmas; it is the conventional designation "nature of an ordinary person.
What is cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*)?
That is to say, the designation "evolution" (*pravṛtti*) is applied to the uninterrupted continuity of cause and effect.
What is "specific determination" (*pratiniyama*)?
It is the designation "specific determination" applied to the various distinctions between causes and effects.
What is association (*samprayoga*)?
It refers to the conventional designation of association based on the correspondence between cause and effect.
What is rapidity (*java*)?
That is to say, "velocity" is a conventional designation for the rapid flow of cause and effect;

"succession" is a conventional designation for the sequential flow of cause and effect one by one. What is this succession? It refers to the sequential flow of each individual instance of cause and effect.
What is time? It is that which is conventionally designated as "time" with respect to the continuous flow and succession of cause and effect.
What is direction?

That is to say, regarding the distinctions of cause and effect in the four cardinal directions—east, west, south, and north—as well as the four intermediate directions and the zenith and nadir, one conventionally designates them as "directions.
What is "number"? It refers to the conventional designation of "number" applied to the individual distinctions among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
What is conjunction?
It is the conventional designation "conjunction" applied to the gathering of causes, effects, and various conditions.
How is the aggregate of consciousness established?
This refers to the distinctions between mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). What is the mind?
It is the *ālayavijñāna*, which contains all seeds perfumed by the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*).
It is also called the *vipākavijñāna* (maturation consciousness) and also called the *ādānavijñāna* (appropriating consciousness), because it is able to accumulate all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
What is the *manas*?

It refers to that which at all times takes the *ālayavijñāna* as its object, having the nature of cogitation and deliberation, and is constantly associated with four afflictions, namely: self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), self-love (*ātma-sneha*), self-pride (*ātma-māna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*).

This manas operates throughout all states—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate—except when the Noble Path is manifest, when one is in the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), or when one is in the stage of an Arhat (aśaikṣabhūmi).
Furthermore, the six consciousnesses take the immediately preceding ceased consciousness as their mental faculty (*manas*).
What constitutes consciousness?
It refers to the six groups of consciousness:
Visual consciousness, auditory consciousness, olfactory consciousness, gustatory consciousness, tactile consciousness, and mental consciousness.
What is visual consciousness?
It is defined as having the nature of discerning forms based upon the eye.
What is auditory consciousness?
It is that which has the nature of cognizing sounds based on the ear.
What is olfactory consciousness?
It has as its nature the discernment of odors based on the nose.
What is tongue-consciousness?
It has as its nature the discernment of tastes based on the tongue.
What is body-consciousness?
It is characterized by the discernment of touch based upon the body.
What is mind-consciousness?

It is defined as having the nature of discerning mental objects (dharma) based upon the mind (manas). How are the elements (dhātu) established? The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) constitutes ten elements:

the eye element (cakṣurdhātu), the form element (rūpadhātu); the ear element (śrotradhātu), the sound element (śabdadhātu); the nose element (ghrāṇadhātu), the odor element (gandhadhātu); the tongue element (jihvādhātu), the taste element (rasadhātu); and the body element (kāyadhātu), the tangible object element (spraṣṭavyadhātu)—along with a portion of the mind element (manodhātu). The aggregates of feeling (vedanāskandha), perception (saṃjñāskandha), and formations (saṃskāraskandha) constitute a portion of the mental-object element (dharmadhātu). The aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) constitutes the seven consciousness elements: namely, the six consciousness elements of the eye and so forth, and the mind element.
Which dharmas of the *dhātu* are not included within the *dharmaskandha*?
They are the various unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas within the *dharmadhātu*.

These unconditioned dharmas are further of eight kinds: namely, the suchness (*tathatā*) of wholesome dharmas, the suchness of unwholesome dharmas, the suchness of indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas, space (*ākāśa*), non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*), analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*), the imperturbable (*āniñjya*), and the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha*).
What is the suchness (*tathatā*) of wholesome phenomena?

It is the nature of selflessness (*anātmatā*), also termed emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), and the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
For what reason is suchness called "suchness"?
This is because its intrinsic nature is without change.
Why is suchness called "selflessness"?
Because it is free from the two kinds of self.
For what reason is suchness called emptiness?
Because it is not traversed by any defilements.
For what reason is suchness called signlessness?
Because all characteristics are quiescent.
For what reason is suchness called the "limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*)?
Because it is the nature of an object that is free from inversion.
For what reason is suchness called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)?
Because it is the sphere of activity of the most supreme noble wisdom.
For what reason is suchness called the dharma-sphere (*dharmadhātu*)?
Because it is the characteristic upon which all the sublime dharmas of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and Buddhas rely.
Just as it is with the suchness of wholesome dharmas, one should know that the suchness of unwholesome dharmas and the suchness of indeterminate dharmas are likewise.
What is space? It is characterized by the absence of form, for it accommodates all conditioned activities.
What is cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)?
That is to say, it is cessation but not dissociation.
What is analytical cessation?
It is that which is both cessation and dissociation.
What is the immovable?
It refers to the cessation of suffering and pleasure when one has already abandoned desire for the Realm of Universal Purity (śubhakṛtsna) but has not yet abandoned desire for the higher realms.
What is the cessation of perception and feeling (saṃjñāvedayitanirodha)?

This refers to the cessation of all non-constant mental states and mental factors, as well as a portion of the constant mental states and mental factors, because one has already abandoned desire for the sphere of nothingness, transcended the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), and is preceded by the mental attention of the temporary cessation of perception.

Furthermore, the five kinds of form, the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations, and these eight unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛtadharma) thus described—these sixteen together are collectively termed the dharma-dhātu.
How are the bases (āyatana) established?

It is said that the ten material elements (dhātu) are the ten material bases; the seven consciousness elements are the mind base (manāyatana); and the mental-object element (dharmadhātu) is the mental-object base (dharmāyatana).

By this principle, all phenomena are subsumed within the three categories of aggregates, elements, and bases, namely: the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), the mental-object element, and the mind base.
As it is said regarding the eye and the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*): if there is an eye, is it also an eye-element?
And if there is an eye-element, is it also an eye?
There may be an eye that is not an eye-element, namely, the final eye of an Arhat.

There may be the element of the eye (cakṣurdhātu) that is not the eye (cakṣus). This refers to: when one is within the eggshell during the stages of the kalala, arbuda, or peśī; when one is in the mother’s womb and has not yet obtained the eye, or has lost it even after obtaining it;
or the cause of the eye possessed by an ordinary being (pṛthagjana) born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
There are cases where one possesses both the eye and the eye-element, namely, in all other states.
There are cases where one possesses neither the eye nor the eye-element, namely, those who have entered the realm of nirvana without remainder, as well as noble ones born in the formless realms.

Just as it is with the eye and the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), so too should the ear, nose, tongue, and body, along with the elements of the ear and so forth, be understood in their entirety according to their respective applications.
If there is mind (*manas*), is there also the mind-element (*manodhātu*)?
If there is a mental element (manodhātu), is it also the mind (manas)?
Or is there that which is the mind but not the mental element? This refers to the final mind of an Arhat.
Or is there that which is the mental element but not the mind? This refers to the causal mind of one who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
There may be both mind and the mind-element, namely in all other states.
There may be neither mind nor the mind-element, namely when one has entered the realm of nirvana without remainder.
If one is born and raised in that realm, does one use the eyes of that realm to see the forms of that realm?
There are cases where one uses the eyes of that realm to see the forms of that realm, and there are also cases where one uses the eyes of another realm.
That is to say, one born in the desire realm sees forms of the desire realm with an eye belonging to the form realm;
or, with an eye from a higher stage of the form realm, sees forms of a lower stage.
Just as it is with the eye in relation to forms, so it is with the ear in relation to sounds.
Just as one who has been born and raised in the desire realm, so too is one who has been born and raised in the form realm.

If one has been born and raised in the desire realm, then by means of the nose, tongue, and body belonging to the desire realm, one smells, tastes, and feels the odors, flavors, and tangibles of the desire realm.
If one is born and grows in the form realm (rūpadhātu), one perceives the tangible objects of one's own level by means of the body belonging to that form realm.
In that realm, odor and taste do not exist by their very nature, because there is freedom from craving for substantial food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra).
By this principle, there are likewise no olfactory or gustatory consciousnesses.
If one is born and grows in the desire realm, one uses the mental consciousness belonging to the desire realm to cognize phenomena of the three realms as well as untainted (anāsrava) phenomena.
Just as it is for one born and raised in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), so it is for one born and raised in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

If one is born and raised in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), by means of a mind belonging to the formless realm, one knows the dharmas of one's own level within the formless realm as well as untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas; or, by means of an untainted mind, one knows the dharmas of the three realms as well as untainted dharmas.
For what reason are the aggregates (skandhas) arranged in this order?
It is because of the stations of consciousness (vijñāna-sthiti), namely the four stations of consciousness and consciousness itself.

Furthermore, it is because each preceding one serves as the basis for the subsequent: one experiences [objects] according to their formal characteristics (rūpa-lakṣaṇa); one cognizes [them] according to how they were experienced; one forms volitions (abhisamskaroti) according to how they were cognized; and one discriminates [them] in various places according to how they were volitionally formed.

Furthermore, the sequence of the aggregates is taught by way of defilement and purification. That is to say, wherever defilement and purification arise—whether through the act of experiencing, grasping signs, and formative activity (saṃskāra), which constitutes defilement and purification, or that which is defiled and that which is purified—it is for this reason that the order of the aggregates is explained.
For what reason are the elements (*dhātu*) arranged in this specific order?
It is because they evolve according to the distinctions of worldly affairs.
How do worldly affairs evolve through such distinctions?

It refers to how people in the world first meet one another; having met, they exchange greetings; having exchanged greetings, they then receive baths, scented ointments, and flower garlands; next, they receive various kinds of excellent food and drink; next, they receive various kinds of bedding and maidservants; and only thereafter does the mental faculty (manodhātu) engage in discrimination in various places. Because the internal bases (ādhyātmikadhātu) follow this sequence, the external bases (bāhyadhātu) are established accordingly, and following this sequence, the consciousness base (vijñānadhātu) is established.
As with the sequence of the elements (*dhātu*), so it is with the bases (*āyatana*).
What is the meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*)?

Whatever form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all that, briefly stated, is called the single aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), because of the sense of accumulation, like a heap of wealth.
In this manner, it extends up to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
Furthermore, they are called aggregates (*skandha*) because their characteristic of suffering is vast, like a great heap of timber.
As stated in the Sūtra:
Thus, because this is the accumulation of the entire mass of suffering,
and because it bears the burden of defilement, it is called a "skandha" (aggregate), just as one carries a load on the shoulder.
What is the meaning of "dhātu" (element)?
It has the sense of being the seed of all phenomena;
it has the sense of maintaining its own specific characteristics;
and it has the sense of maintaining the nature of cause and effect.
Furthermore, regarding the meaning of "basis" (*āyatana*) as that which encompasses the distinct meanings of all phenomena:
what is the meaning of "basis"?
The meaning of being a gateway for the growth and arising of consciousness is the meaning of "basis."
As the Buddha has taught:
form is like a mass of foam, sensation is like a floating bubble, perception is like a mirage, mental formations are like a plantain tree, and consciousness is like a magical illusion.
For what reason is form like a mass of foam, and so on, up to consciousness being like a magical illusion?
Because they are without self, devoid of purity, of little flavor, not solid, and not real.
