Part Two of Chapter One: The Three Dharmas, within the Section on Past Events. Furthermore, what is the detailed analysis of the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and bases (āyatana)?
The summary verse says:
Substantial existence and so forth, the knowable and so forth; Form and so forth, the outflows and so forth, the arisen and so forth;
The past and so forth, the various conditions and so forth— What, how many kinds, and for what purpose?
Among the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, what is substantially existent?
How many are substantially existent?
For what purpose is substantial existence investigated?
This means that those faculties and objects which do not depend on verbal designations are real entities (*dravyasat*).
All such things are indeed real entities.
One examines real entities in order to abandon the attachment to a real self (*ātman*).
What is provisional existence?
How many things are provisionally existent?
For what purpose is provisional existence investigated?
This means that those other faculties and objects which depend upon designations are of the nature of the conventionally existent (*prajñaptisat*).
All things are conventionally existent.
One examines what is conventionally existent in order to relinquish attachment to a self that is substantially real (*dravyasat*).
What is conventional existence?
How many things are conventionally existent?
For what purpose is conventional existence investigated?
That which has the defiled as its object is the meaning of conventional existence (*saṃvṛtisat*).
All things are conventionally existent.
One examines conventional existence in order to abandon attachment to a self characterized by defilement.
What is ultimate existence?
How many things are ultimately existent?
For what purpose is ultimate existence investigated?
That which is the object of purification is the meaning of ultimate existence.
All things are ultimately existent.
One examines ultimate existence in order to abandon attachment to a self characterized by purity.
What is the knowable?
How many are the knowables?
For what purpose is the knowable investigated?
That is to say, there are five kinds of objects of knowledge (*jñeya*):

first, matter (*rūpa*); second, mind (*citta*); third, mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*); fourth, formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*); and fifth, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

In this regard, whether it be the locus of affliction and purification, that which is afflicted and that which is purified, that which afflicts and that which purifies, these particular states, or this very nature of purity—it is because of relying upon all these that they are entirely objects of knowledge (*jñeya*).

In this context, "form" refers to the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), comprising the ten material elements (*dhātu*), the ten material bases (*āyatana*), and all forms subsumed within the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and the base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
"Mind" refers to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), comprising the seven consciousness elements and the mind base (*manāyatana*).

Mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) refer to the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), the associated portion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*), and one part of the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).

Non-associated formations (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*) refer to the non-associated aggregate of formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*) and one part of the sphere of phenomena and the sphere of mental objects.
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) refers to a portion of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) and the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*).

Furthermore, regarding "knowable phenomena" (*jñeya-dharma*): they are called knowable objects because they are the domain of the wisdom of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-jñāna*), the domain of the wisdom of reasoning (*yukti-jñāna*), the domain of the wisdom of non-distraction (*avikṣepa-jñāna*), the domain of internally realized wisdom (*pratyātma-jñāna*), the domain of the wisdom of other-nature (*parabhāva-jñāna*), the domain of lower wisdom (*hīna-jñāna*), the domain of superior wisdom (*viśiṣṭa-jñāna*), the domain of the wisdom of weariness (*udvega-jñāna*), the domain of the wisdom of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), the domain of the wisdom of non-birth (*ajāti-jñāna*), the domain of the wisdom of wisdom (*jñānajñāna*), the domain of ultimate wisdom (*niṣṭhā-jñāna*), and the domain of the wisdom of great purpose (*mahārtha-jñāna*). These are the meanings of the knowable.
All things are objects of knowledge (*jñeya*).
One examines the objects of knowledge in order to abandon the attachment to a self that is a knower or a seer.
What is it that is cognized?
How many are the objects of cognition?
For what purpose are they investigated as objects of cognition?

They are the objects of cognition in the sense of being non-conceptual, being conceptual, being causes, being transformations, being characteristics, being produced from characteristics, being the remedial and the remediable, and being subtle distinctions.
All things are objects of cognition.
One examines the objects of cognition in order to abandon attachment to a self that is a seer and so forth.
What is it that is thoroughly penetrated?
What is that which is thoroughly penetrated?
For what purpose does one contemplate that which is thoroughly penetrated?

It is said: because of transformation, because of following what is heard, because of entering into practice, because of coming, because of going, and because of renunciation—this is the meaning of that which is thoroughly penetrated.
All these are what is thoroughly penetrated.
One investigates what is thoroughly penetrated in order to abandon the attachment to a self possessed of majestic power.
What is that which possesses form?
What is that which possesses form (*rūpin*)? For what purpose is that which possesses form investigated?

It is because of its intrinsic nature as form; because it depends on the primary elements (*mahābhūta*); because it is an accumulation of delight; because it has a location; because it pervades space; because its location can be described; because it moves within locations; because it shares a common range with two [senses]; because it is connected; because it follows along; because it is manifest; because it is subject to transformation and decay; because it displays itself; because it is established through accumulation; because it pertains to the external sphere; because it pertains to the internal sphere; because it is long-lasting; because it is limited; because it is momentary; and because it is demonstrable—these are the meanings of "possessing form."
All are possessed of form.
Alternatively, as appropriate, one contemplates that which possesses form in order to abandon attachment to a self that possesses form.
What is that which is without form?
How many are formless?
For what purpose is the formless investigated?
That which is the opposite of having form is the meaning of "formless."
All are formless. Alternatively, one contemplates the formless as appropriate in order to abandon attachment to a self that is formless.
What is "with visibility"?
How many are with visibility?
For what purpose is "with visibility" investigated?
That which is the objective domain of the eye is the meaning of "with visibility"; the other distinctions are as explained in the section on "possessing form."
All are with visibility (*sanidarśana*).
Alternatively, as appropriate, one contemplates visibility in order to abandon attachment to a self within the objective domain of the eye.
What is non-visibility (*anidarśana*)?
How many are non-visible?
For what purpose is the non-visible investigated?
That which is the opposite of the visible is the meaning of the non-visible.
All are non-visible.
Alternatively, as appropriate, one contemplates them as non-visible in order to abandon the attachment to a self that is not an object of the eye.
What is "with resistance" (sapratigha)?
How many are with resistance?
For what purpose is there an investigation into that which has resistance?
It is said that all things that are visible are with resistance.
Furthermore, it is called "possessing resistance" (*sapratigha*) for three reasons: by way of its nature, by way of accumulation, and by way of lack of cultivation.
As for its nature, it means that all material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) act as mutual obstructions and are mutually obstructed.
"Accumulated" refers to that which is composed of atoms and above.
"Unrefined" refers to matter that does not function with mastery over samādhi.
Furthermore, the sense of being "impeded" (sapratigha) means being a basis for harm.
All are with resistance (*sapratigha*).
Alternatively, they are examined as being with resistance as appropriate, in order to abandon the attachment to a self that is not omnipresent (*asarvatraga*).
What is without resistance (*apratigha*)?
How many are non-resistant?
For what purpose is non-resistance investigated?
That which is the opposite of resistance is the meaning of non-resistance.
All are non-resistant (*apratigha*).
Alternatively, they are observed as non-resistant as appropriate, in order to abandon attachment to a pervasive self (*sarvatraga-ātman*).
What is with-outflow (*sāsrava*)?
How many are with outflows (*sāsrava*)?
For what purpose are they examined as being with outflows?

They are defined as "with outflows" by virtue of: the nature of the outflows themselves; association with the outflows; being bound by the outflows; being pursued by the outflows; being conducive to the outflows; and being of the same category as the outflows. This is the meaning of "being with outflows."

The five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), fifteen elements (*dhātu*), ten bases (*āyatana*) in their entirety, and a portion of three elements and two bases are with outflows (*sāsrava*).
One contemplates what is with outflows in order to abandon attachment to a self that is conjoined with outflows.
What is the untainted (*anāsrava*)?
How many are untainted?
For what purpose is the untainted investigated?
That which is contrary to the contaminated (*sāsrava*) is the meaning of the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
The five aggregates of non-appropriation (*anupādānaskandha*) in their entirety, as well as a portion of three elements (*dhātu*) and two bases (*āyatana*), are uncontaminated.
One examines the uncontaminated in order to abandon attachment to a self that is free from outflows.
What is "with conflict"?
How many things are "with conflict"?
For what purpose is there an investigation into that which is "with conflict"?

That is to say, based on such greed, hatred, and delusion, one grasps swords and staves and initiates all forms of combat, litigation, and contention. Because it is their intrinsic nature, because it is associated with them, because it is bound by them, because it follows after them, because it conforms to them, and because it is of their same category, this is the meaning of "being contentious."
To whatever extent there are outflows (*āsrava*), to that same extent there are disputes (*saraṇa*).
One examines what has dispute in order to abandon attachment to a self associated with dispute.
What is without dispute (*araṇa*)?
How many are the bases of non-contention?
For what purpose are they investigated?
That which is contrary to contention is the meaning of non-contention.
To the extent that there is such a measure of the untainted (*anāsrava*), so too is there for the absence of contention (*araṇā*).
One contemplates the absence of contention in order to abandon attachment to a self that is free from contention.
How is it defiled?
What is "existence-tainted" (*sāmiṣa*)?
For what purpose is existence-tainted investigated?

It refers to being defiled by attachment to one's own future existence (*punarbhava*) due to such greed, hatred, and delusion. It has the sense of being "existence-tainted" because of its intrinsic nature, its association with it, its bondage by it, its pursuit by it, its conformity to it, and its belonging to its category.
To whatever extent there is contention, to that same extent there is defilement.
One examines what is defiled in order to abandon the attachment to a self conjoined with defilement.
What is undefiled?
How many are undefiled?
For what purpose is the investigation of the undefiled undertaken?
That which is contrary to being defiled is the meaning of "undefiled."
To whatever extent there is non-contention (*araṇā*), to that same extent there is freedom from defilement (*asaṃkleśa*).
One examines freedom from defilement in order to abandon attachment to a self that is free from defilement.
What is reliance on indulgence (*gardhāśrita*)?
How many are based on attachment to worldly enjoyment (*ādhyavasāna-niśrita*)?
For what purpose is one to contemplate that which is based on attachment to worldly enjoyment?

It refers to being stained by and attached to the five objects of desire (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*) due to such greed, hatred, and delusion. By virtue of their intrinsic nature, their association, their bondage, their persistence, their conformity, and their category, this is the meaning of being "based on attachment to worldly enjoyment."
To whatever extent there is defilement, to that same extent there is reliance on indulgence (*gardha*).
In order to abandon the attachment that clings to indulgence as being conjoined with a self, one contemplates reliance on indulgence.
What is reliance on renunciation?
How many are reliance on renunciation?
For what purpose does one contemplate reliance on renunciation?
This means that being contrary to the characteristic of attachment is the meaning of renunciation (*naiṣkramya*).
To the extent that there is non-defilement, so too is there renunciation.
One examines renunciation in order to abandon the clinging to a self that is free from attachment.
What is the conditioned?
How many are conditioned?
For what purpose is the conditioned investigated?
That is to say, if a phenomenon possesses arising, ceasing, abiding, and change, it can be known as having the characteristic of being conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
All things are conditioned, with the sole exception of one portion of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) and the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*).
In order to abandon attachment to an impermanent self, one contemplates the conditioned.
What is the unconditioned?
How many are unconditioned?
For what purpose is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) examined?
It means that being the opposite of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is the meaning of the unconditioned.
A portion of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) and the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*) is unconditioned.
In order to abandon attachment to a permanent self, one contemplates the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Should the five aggregates that are without grasping (*anupādāna*) be said to be conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned?
One should not say that it is conditioned or unconditioned.

Why? Because it is not produced by any karma or afflictions, one should not say it is conditioned; yet, because it is not something other than what is produced by karma and afflictions, one should not say it is unconditioned.
Because they manifest or do not manifest according to one's wishes, they should not be called unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
As the Blessed One said:
"There are two kinds of phenomena (*dharma*): namely, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)."
Why is it said that this Dharma is neither conditioned nor unconditioned?
If, by a certain meaning, it is called conditioned, it is not by that same meaning called unconditioned;
if, by a certain meaning, it is called unconditioned, it is not by that same meaning called conditioned.
Based on this principle, only two types are taught.
What is the mundane? How many are mundane?
For what purpose is the world investigated?
That which is comprised within the three realms, as well as that which appears as resembling them and is subsequently attained by supramundane wisdom—this is the meaning of "the world."
A portion of the aggregates (*skandha*), fifteen elements (*dhātu*), ten bases (*āyatana*) in their entirety, and a portion of three elements and two bases constitute the world (*loka*).
One examines the world in order to abandon attachment to a self that is the basis of the world.
What is supramundane?
How many are supramundane?
For what purpose is the supramundane investigated?

This means that because it serves as the antidote to the three realms, being without inversion, without conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and without discrimination, it is the meaning of supramundane non-discrimination.
Furthermore, that which is subsequently attained after emerging from the supramundane is also called "supramundane."
Because it relies upon that which transcends the world, it has the meaning of "transcending the world.
A portion of the aggregates (*skandha*), as well as a portion of three elements (*dhātu*) and two bases (*āyatana*), are what transcend the world.
One examines that which transcends the world in order to abandon attachment to a self that exists independently.
What is that which has already arisen?
How many things have already arisen?
For what purpose is that which has already arisen investigated?
That is to say, the past and the present constitute the meaning of "already arisen.
A portion of all [phenomena] is already arisen.
One examines what is already arisen in order to abandon attachment to a non-eternal self.

Furthermore, there are twenty-four kinds of "already arisen": namely, initially arisen; continuously arisen; nurturedly arisen; supportively arisen; transformatively arisen; maturely arisen; regressive arisen; progressive arisen; pure arisen; impure arisen; functionally arisen; with-seed arisen; seedless arisen; arisen as a manifestation of sovereign mastery over images; successively arisen; momentarily disintegrating arisen; separated-and-reunited arisen; arisen in different states; arisen in birth and death; arisen in formation and destruction; arisen at the prior time; arisen at the time of death; arisen at the intermediate time; and arisen at the time of continuity.
What is the unarisen?
How many are unarisen?
For what purpose is the unarisen investigated?
This refers to future phenomena and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), which have the meaning of "not yet arisen.
A portion of all phenomena is "not yet arisen.
One examines what is not yet arisen in order to abandon attachment to a permanent self (*ātman*).
Furthermore, that which is contrary to having already arisen is the meaning of not yet having arisen.
How can it be an apprehender?
How many are apprehenders?
For what purpose is the grasper (*grāhaka*) examined?
It means that the material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*), as well as the mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*), have the nature of being the grasper.

The three aggregates (*skandha*) in their entirety, a portion of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), the twelve bases (*dhātu*) and six sense-fields (*āyatana*) in their entirety, and a portion of the dharma-base (*dharma-dhātu*) and dharma-field (*dharma-āyatana*), are the grasper.
In order to abandon attachment to the self that experiences, one examines the grasper (*grāhaka*).

Furthermore, there are four kinds of graspers: the grasper that does not reach [its object], the grasper that reaches [its object], the grasper of distinct objects in their own-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) at the present moment, and the grasper of all objects at all times in both their own-characteristics and common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, because consciousness and the other factors arise through their conjunction, the "grasper" (subject) is provisionally established.
What is the "grasped" (object)?
How many are the grasped?
For what purpose is the apprehended object (*grāhya*) examined?
It is because all that is the apprehending subject (*grāhaka*) is also the apprehended object.
Alternatively, there are apprehended objects that are not apprehending subjects, namely, those objects that are exclusively the domain of the apprehension itself.
All these are the grasped (grāhya).
One examines the grasped in order to abandon attachment to a self that is the objective sphere.
What is the external gate?
How many are the external doors?
For what purpose does one contemplate the external doors?
It means that the phenomena bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu) constitute the meaning of the external doors.

Excluding the wisdom arising from hearing and reflection based on the Buddha’s teachings, as well as the mind and mental factors subsumed under the practice in accordance with those teachings, all of the four elements and two bases, along with one portion of the rest subsumed under the desire realm, constitute the external door.
In order to abandon attachment to a self that is not free from desire, one examines the external door.
What is the internal door?
How many are the internal doors?
For what purpose is the internal door (ajjhatta-dvāra) examined?
It means that being the opposite of the external door is the meaning of the internal door.
With the exception of the four elements, two bases in their entirety, and a portion of the remainder, these constitute the internal door.
In order to abandon attachment to a self that is free from desire, one examines the internal sphere.
What is defilement?
How many things are defiled?
For what purpose is defilement investigated?
It refers to unwholesome (*akuśala*) and obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) phenomena; this is the meaning of defilement.

As for the obscured-unspecified, it refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*) associated with the universal mental faculty (*sarvatraga-manas*), as well as the various afflictions bound to the realms of form and formlessness.
A portion of the aggregates, ten elements, and four bases is afflicted (*kliṣṭa*).
One examines what is afflicted in order to abandon the attachment that conceives of a self as being conjoined with afflictions.
What is non-afflicted?
What is non-defiled?
For what purpose is it examined as non-defiled?
It refers to wholesome and unobscured-neutral phenomena; this is the meaning of being non-defiled.
The eight elements and eight bases in their entirety, as well as a portion of the aggregates and the remaining elements and bases, are non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*).
One examines them as non-defiled in order to abandon attachment to a self that is free from afflictions.
What is the past? How many things are the past?
For what purpose is the past investigated?

That is to say, it is the meaning of "past" because its own-characteristics have already arisen and ceased; because its causes and fruits have already been experienced; because the functional activity of defilement and purification has already subsided; because the gathering of causes has already disintegrated; because its fruits and own-characteristics exist and yet do not exist; because it is characterized by recollective conceptualization; because attachment constitutes the characteristic of defilement; and because relinquishment constitutes the characteristic of purification. This is the meaning of the past.
A portion of all [phenomena] is past.
One examines the past in order to abandon attachment to a self that undergoes transmigration.
What is the future?
How many are the future? For what purpose is the future investigated? It is because they possess causes that have not yet arisen;

because their own-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) have not yet been attained; because cause and effect have not yet been experienced; because the natures of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*) have not yet manifested; because their causes and own-characteristics exist yet do not exist; because there is a longing for the characteristics of affliction; and because there is no longing for the characteristics of purification—this is the meaning of the future.
One portion of all [dharmas] is future.
One examines the future in order to abandon attachment to a self that undergoes transmigration.
What is the present?
How many are present? For what purpose is the present investigated? It is defined as follows:

because its own-characteristic has already arisen but not yet ceased; because its causes and effects have been experienced or not yet experienced; because defilement and purification are currently manifesting; because it can manifest the characteristics of the past and future; and because its activity is currently present—these are the meanings of the present.
All [conditioned phenomena] are partially present.
One examines the present in order to abandon attachment to a self that undergoes transmigration.
Why are the past, future, and present described as "conventional designations" (*adhivacana*) and "entities" (*vastu*), whereas nirvāṇa and so forth are not?
Because that which is personally realized within is inexpressible, and because only the past, future, and present serve as the basis for verbal expression.
What is wholesome?
How many are wholesome?
For what purpose is the wholesome (*kuśala*) examined? It is the meaning of "wholesome" by way of:

intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), association (*saṃprayoga*), accompaniment (*pṛṣṭhasthāna*), origination (*samutthāna*), ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), birth-attainment (*upapatti-labdha*), application (*prāyogika*), manifest offering (*abhimukha-pūjā*), benefit (*anugraha*), attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), antidote (*pratipakṣa*), tranquility (*upaśama*), and outflow (*niṣyanda*). This is the meaning of the wholesome.
A portion of the five aggregates, ten elements, and four bases is wholesome (*kuśala*).
One examines what is wholesome in order to abandon attachment to phenomena as being conjoined with a self.
What is wholesome by its own nature (*svabhāva-kuśala*)?
This refers to the eleven mental factors (caitasika-dharma), beginning with faith.
What is the characteristic of their association with the wholesome?
It is the dharmas that are associated with them.
What is the goodness that follows along?
It refers to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of those very same phenomena.
What is the goodness that initiates?
This refers to the bodily and vocal actions produced by that [wholesome mind].
What is ultimate wholesomeness?
It is suchness (*tathatā*).
What is the wholesome acquired at birth?

It refers to those very wholesome dharmas which, due to prior habitual practice, result in such a retribution; by virtue of this intrinsic nature, one spontaneously and effortlessly dwells with delight in that state without the need for deliberation.
What is the wholesome of application?

It refers to relying upon and associating with virtuous persons, hearing the true Dharma, attending to it correctly, and cultivating pure wholesome dharmas through practice in accordance with the Dharma.
What is the excellence of manifest offering?
It refers to visualizing the Tathāgata and constructing shrines or painting sacred images;
or visualizing the True Dharma and transcribing the treasury of the teachings to perform acts of worship.
What is the excellence of benefiting?
It refers to benefiting all sentient beings by means of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
What is the excellence of drawing in?

That is to say, because of the meritorious action consisting of giving and the meritorious action consisting of ethical discipline, one brings about the ripening of happiness in rebirth in the heavens, brings about rebirth in a wealthy and noble family, and brings about that which is conducive to the dharmas of purification.
What is the wholesome that serves as an antidote?

It refers to the antidote of revulsion and destruction, the antidote of abandonment, the antidote of maintenance, the antidote of distancing, the antidote of suppression, the antidote of dissociation, the antidote to the obscuration of afflictions, and the antidote to the obscuration of the knowable.
What is the excellence of tranquility?

It refers to the permanent abandonment of greed, the permanent abandonment of hatred, the permanent abandonment of delusion, and the permanent abandonment of all afflictions; it refers to the cessation of perception and feeling, the nirvāṇa-realm with remainder, the nirvāṇa-realm without remainder, and the nirvāṇa-realm of non-abiding.
What is the virtue of natural outflow (*niṣyanda*)?

It refers to those who have already attained tranquility and, through the predominant power of this [attainment], give rise to superior qualities such as the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), which are common or uncommon to both mundane and supramundane realms.
What is the unwholesome?
How many are unwholesome?
For what purpose is the unwholesome investigated?

The meaning of "unwholesome" is defined by way of: intrinsic nature, association, persistence, origination, ultimate truth, acquisition by birth, application, manifest offering, harm, attraction, that which is to be countered, and obstruction.
A portion of the five aggregates, ten elements, and four bases is unwholesome (*akuśala*).
One examines the unwholesome in order to abandon attachment to a self that is conjoined with what is non-dharmic.
What is unwholesome by way of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)?

This refers to those remaining afflictions and secondary afflictions capable of giving rise to unwholesome conduct, excluding those associated with the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*) as well as the afflictions of the form and formless realms.
What are the characteristics of that which is connected to the unwholesome?
This refers to those factors associated with these very afflictions and secondary afflictions.
What is that which follows along with the unwholesome?
It refers to their respective habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
What is unwholesome by way of origination?
It refers to the bodily and vocal actions produced by that [unwholesome mind].
What is unwholesome in the ultimate sense?
This refers to all processes of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
What is innate unwholesomeness (*upapattilābhika-akuśala*)?

It refers to obtaining such a karmic maturation (*vipāka*) through the habituation to unwholesome states, by virtue of which one spontaneously and effortlessly dwells in unwholesomeness due to that very nature.
What is unwholesome preparatory action?
It refers to relying upon and associating with unwholesome persons, hearing incorrect teachings, engaging in improper mental attention, and performing unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind.
What is unwholesome manifest worship?

It refers to having first conceived the thought of taking refuge in one class of celestial beings, and then—motivated either by an intent to harm or by an evil intent—establishing a shrine and extensively engaging in acts of worship, thereby causing immeasurable multitudes to plant vast stores of non-merit.
What is unwholesome action that causes harm?
It refers to the various forms of misconduct of body, speech, and mind arising in all circumstances.
What is unwholesome action that leads to [rebirth]?

This refers to having committed various unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind, which then project or complete the acquisition of undesirable results and maturations in either the miserable realms or the happy realms.
What are the unwholesome factors that are to be countered?
This refers to those phenomena that are the objects of counteraction for their respective remedies.
What are the unwholesome factors that constitute obstacles?
They are those phenomena capable of obstructing the various categories of wholesome qualities.
What is the indeterminate?
How many are indeterminate?
For what purpose is the indeterminate investigated?

That is to say, it is the meaning of "indeterminate" (avyākṛta) by virtue of its intrinsic nature, its association, its persistence, its origination, its ultimate sense, its acquisition at birth, its application, its manifest offering, its benefit, its enjoyment, its attraction, its antidote, its tranquility, and its outflow.
The eight elements (*dhātu*) and eight bases (*āyatana*) in their entirety, as well as a portion of the remaining aggregates, elements, and bases, are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
One examines the indeterminate in order to abandon attachment to a self that is distinct from both dharma and adharma.
What is the indeterminate by nature (*svabhāva-avyākṛta*)?

It refers to the eight bases of form, the mental concomitants, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*), and the sets of names, phrases, and phonemes (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*).
What is the indeterminate associated with connection?
It refers to all mind and mental factors, comprised by the sets of names, phrases, and phonemes, belonging to one who possesses a mind that is neither defiled nor pure.
What is the indeterminate that follows along?
It refers to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of those very conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*).
What is the indeterminate that initiates?
This refers to the bodily and vocal actions produced by those minds and mental factors that have been grasped [by craving].
What is the ultimate neutral?
It refers to space and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
What is the indeterminate acquired at birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika-avyākṛta*)?
It refers to the maturation (*vipāka*) of all unwholesome (*akuśala*) and impure wholesome (*sāsrava-kuśala*) dharmas.
What is the indeterminate of application (*prāyogika-avyākṛta*)?
This refers to the modes of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and the arts and crafts (*śailpasthānika*) belonging to a mind that is neither defiled nor wholesome.
What is the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) present offering?

It is as when someone, with the intention of taking refuge in one of the various classes of celestial beings, builds a shrine or temple and performs acts of worship while remaining free from the intent to kill and free from false views, such that immeasurable multitudes do not produce either merit or demerit at such a place.
What is the indeterminate [action] that is beneficial?
It refers, for example, to when someone bestows gifts upon their own servants, wives, children, and so forth, with a mind that is neither defiled nor pure.
What is neutral through enjoyment?
It refers to when someone, with a mind that is neither discerning nor defiled, enjoys material requisites.
What is neutral through acquisition?

That is to say, there is someone who, through habitual practice in a field of craftsmanship, draws forth and acquires a body of such characteristics in a future life; by means of this body, they swiftly reach mastery in that field of craftsmanship.
What is the indeterminate of counteraction?
It refers to a case where someone, for the sake of curing an illness and attaining well-being, takes medicine with a mind of careful discernment.
What is the indeterminate of tranquility?
This refers to the various afflictions and so forth of the form and formless realms, which are concealed and suppressed by śamatha.
What is the outflow-neutral (niṣyanda-avyākṛta)?
It refers to the category of mental states co-arising with the mind of transformation (nirmāṇa-citta).
Furthermore, there is the manifestation of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena. What is this?
It refers to what is manifested by Buddhas and Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have attained the ultimate consummation, for the purpose of benefiting all sentient beings.
One should know that herein not a single dharma can be found as truly existent.
What is bound to the desire realm?
How many are bound to the desire realm?
For what purpose is the connection to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) examined?
It means that all wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena belonging to one who has not yet abandoned desire constitute the meaning of being connected to the desire realm.
The four elements, two bases in their entirety, and a portion of the remaining aggregates, elements, and bases are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
One examines what is bound to the desire realm in order to abandon the attachment to a self that has not yet transcended the desires of the desire realm.
What is that which is bound to the realm of form?
How many things are bound to the realm of form?
For what purpose is that which is bound to the realm of form investigated?

This refers to all wholesome and indeterminate dharmas belonging to one who has already abandoned desire for the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) but has not yet abandoned desire for the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*); this is the meaning of being "bound to the realm of form.
Excluding the four elements and two bases previously mentioned, a portion of the remaining aggregates, elements, and bases constitutes that which is bound to the realm of form.
In order to abandon attachment to the self that clings to freedom from desire for the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), one examines what is bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
What is bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?
How many things are bound to the formless realm?
For what purpose is the connection with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) examined?

It refers to all wholesome and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas belonging to one who has already abandoned desire for the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-vītarāga*) but has not yet abandoned desire for the formless realm; this is the meaning of being connected with the formless realm.
A portion of the three realms, two bases, and four aggregates is bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-saṃprayukta*).
One examines what is bound to the formless realm in order to abandon attachment to a self that is free from desire for the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-vairāgya*).

Furthermore, there is partial detachment from desire, complete detachment from desire, penetration of detachment from desire, suppression of detachment from desire, and permanent destruction of detachment from desire.

There are also ten kinds of detachment from desire: namely, detachment from desire by nature, detachment from desire through harm, detachment from desire through sustenance, detachment from desire through predominance, detachment from desire through delusion, detachment from desire through antidote, detachment from desire through full knowledge, detachment from desire through permanent abandonment, detachment from desire that has something superior, and detachment from desire that has nothing superior.
What is detachment by nature?
It is the state of aversion toward painful feelings and those phenomena conducive to painful feelings.
What is detachment through harm?
This means that when one who indulges in sensual desires has relieved their feverish distress, a state of aversion arises.
What is the sustaining power of detachment from desire?
It is like the state of aversion toward fine delicacies that arises after one has eaten to satiety.
What is superior detachment from desire?
It refers to the state of aversion toward inferior objects once one has attained a superior state.
What is deluded detachment from desire?
This refers to the state of aversion toward the realm of nirvāṇa produced by foolish commoners.
What is the antidote for the abandonment of desire?
It is the severing of all afflictions by means of both mundane and supramundane paths.
What is the thorough knowledge of detachment?
It refers to the state of aversion toward the phenomena of the three realms that arises in one who has already attained the path of vision.
What is the dispassion of permanent abandonment?
It refers to the nature of aversion and turning away that arises after one has permanently abandoned the various afflictions of each respective stage (*bhūmi*).
What is the dispassion that has something superior to it?
This refers to the detachment from desire possessed by worldly beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.
What is supreme detachment from desire?
It is the detachment from desire possessed by buddhas and bodhisattvas, for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings.
What is the state of one in training (*śaikṣa*)? How many are those in training?
For what purpose is the state of one in training investigated?
All wholesome dharmas belonging to one who seeks liberation are the meaning of "in training" (*śaikṣa*).
Ten elements (*dhātu*), four bases (*āyatana*), and a portion of the aggregates (*skandha*) constitute that which is in training.
One examines what is in training in order to abandon attachment to a self that seeks liberation.
What is the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*)?
How many factors are of no-more-learning?
For what purpose is the state of no-more-learning investigated?
The meaning of "one beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*) refers to all wholesome qualities belonging to one who has already attained perfection in the various points of training (*śikṣāpada*).
One investigates the state of being beyond training in order to abandon attachment to a self that is already liberated.
What is that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
How many are neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
For what purpose is the investigation of the neither-learner-nor-non-learner undertaken?

This refers to all wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate dharmas belonging to ordinary worldlings; the defiled and indeterminate dharmas of those in training (śaikṣa); and the indeterminate dharmas as well as the unconditioned dharmas (asaṃskṛta) of those beyond training (aśaikṣa). This is the meaning of "neither in training nor beyond training" (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa).

The eight elements (*dhātu*) and eight bases (*āyatana*) in their entirety, as well as a portion of the remaining aggregates (*skandha*), elements, and bases, are neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
One examines what is neither-learner-nor-non-learner in order to abandon attachment to a self that is not liberated.
What is abandoned by vision?
How many are abandoned by vision?
For what purpose is that which is abandoned by vision investigated?

This refers to the defiled views and doubts arising from conceptual discrimination, as well as the objects of those views and doubts; the afflictions and secondary afflictions consisting of wrong conduct directed toward those views and so forth; the bodily, vocal, and mental actions instigated by those views and so forth; and all the aggregates, elements, and bases of the evil destinies and so on—these constitute the meaning of "to be abandoned by seeing."
A portion of all [phenomena] is to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*).
One examines what is to be abandoned by insight in order to relinquish attachment to a self that is complete in its views.
What is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?
How many are to be abandoned by cultivation?
For what purpose are those to be abandoned by cultivation investigated?

It means that after attaining the path of seeing, those contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) which are contrary to what is to be abandoned by seeing are the meaning of "to be abandoned by cultivation."
A portion of all [phenomena] is to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
One examines what is to be abandoned through cultivation in order to relinquish attachment to a self that is perfected through cultivation.
What is not to be abandoned?
How many are not to be abandoned?
For what purpose are those that are not to be abandoned investigated?
It refers to all untainted (anāsrava) phenomena, excluding the factors conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya); these are not to be abandoned.
A portion of the ten realms, the four bases, and the aggregates is not to be abandoned.
One examines what is not to be abandoned in order to relinquish attachment to a perfected self.
What is dependently originated?
How many are dependently originated?
For what purpose is dependent origination investigated?

It is for the sake of its characteristics, for the sake of the analysis of its members, for the sake of the concise inclusion of its members, for the sake of establishing the conditions of its members, for the sake of establishing the functions of its members, for the sake of the inclusion of its members within the defilements, for the sake of its meaning, for the sake of its profundity, for the sake of its differentiation, and for the sake of its direct and reverse order; such is the meaning of dependent origination.
All things are dependently originated, with the sole exception of that portion of the dharma-realm and the dharma-base consisting of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
One contemplates dependent origination in order to abandon the attachment to a self and phenomena that have no cause or an unequal cause.
By what characteristics?

It means that because it is dependently originated through non-action, because it is dependently originated through impermanence, and because it is dependently originated through functional efficacy—these are the characteristics of dependent origination.
By what analysis of its branches?
That is to say, dependent origination is analyzed into twelve factors.
What are these twelve? They are:
ignorance, formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and old age and death.
What are the summarized branches? They are:
the projecting branches, the projected branches, the producing branches, and the produced branches.
The projecting branches consist of ignorance (*avidyā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
The "projected factors" (ākṣepaka-aṅga) refer to name-and-form (nāmarūpa), the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana), contact (sparśa), and feeling (vedanā).
The "generative factors" (abhinirvartaka-aṅga) refer to craving (tṛṣṇā), grasping (upādāna), and becoming (bhava).
The "generated factors" (abhinirvṛtti-aṅga) refer to birth (jāti) and old age and death (jarāmaraṇa).
What is the establishment of the conditions for the members?

It refers to the establishment of the conditions for the members—according to their respective applications—by way of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), by way of projection (*ākṣepa*), by way of mental attention (*manasikāra*), and by way of coexistence (*sahabhū*).
What is the establishment by way of the functions of the members?
It is said that ignorance has two kinds of functions:
first, it causes sentient beings to be deluded regarding existence (*bhava*).
Second, it serves as a condition for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
Volitional formations have two types of functions:
first, they cause sentient beings to undergo various distinctions within the realms of existence; [second, they serve as a condition for consciousness].
Second, it acts as a condition for consciousness.
Due to perfuming, consciousness has two kinds of functions:
first, it maintains the karmic bonds of all sentient beings; [second, it projects future existence].
Second, it acts as a condition for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Name-and-form has two functions:
first, it sustains the individual existence of sentient beings; [second, it serves as the basis for the six sense bases].
Second, it serves as a condition for the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
The six sense bases have two functions:
first, they bring about the complete integration of the individual existence (*ātman*) of sentient beings.
Second, it serves as a condition for contact.
Contact has two functions:
first, it causes sentient beings to circulate within the objects they experience; [second, it serves as a condition for feeling].
Second, it serves as a condition for sensation (*vedanā*).
Sensation has two functions:
first, it causes sentient beings to flow through the cycle of existence within the fruits they experience.
Second, it serves as a condition for craving.
Craving has two functions:
first, it draws sentient beings into the cycle of birth and death; [second, it causes them to cling].
Second, it serves as the condition for grasping (*upādāna*).
Grasping has two functions:
first, it brings about subsequent existence (*punarbhava*), causing sentient beings to give rise to consciousness accompanied by grasping (*sopādāna-vijñāna*).
Second, it serves as a condition for existence (*bhava*).
Existence has two functions:
first, it causes the subsequent existence of sentient beings to manifest.
Second, it acts as a condition for birth (*jāti*).
Birth has two types of functions:

first, it causes the successive arising of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*) in sentient beings; [and second, it serves as the basis for aging and death].
Second, it acts as a condition for aging and death.
Aging and death have two functions:
first, they repeatedly cause the temporal state of sentient beings to undergo transformation; [the second is to bring about their dissolution].
Second, they cause the life-span of sentient beings to undergo change.
Which members are subsumed under defilement?
Namely, ignorance, craving, and grasping; these are subsumed under the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*).
Whether it be volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), or existence (*bhava*), these are subsumed under the defilement of karma (*karmasaṃkleśa*).
The remainder are subsumed under the defilement of birth (*janmasaṃkleśa*). For what reason?

That is to say, the meaning of being without an agent, the meaning of having causes, the meaning of being devoid of a sentient being, the meaning of dependent origination, the meaning of lacking functional activity, the meaning of impermanence, the meaning of momentariness, the meaning of the uninterrupted continuity of cause and effect, the meaning of the correspondence between cause and effect, the meaning of the differentiation of cause and effect, and the meaning of the determination of cause and effect—these are the meanings of dependent origination.
What is meant by "profound"?

It refers to the profundity of causes, the profundity of characteristics, the profundity of arising, the profundity of abiding, and the profundity of transformation; such is the meaning of profundity.

Furthermore, although all dependently originated phenomena perish moment by moment, their persistence can be apprehended; although there are no active conditions, functional conditions can be apprehended; although they are devoid of sentient beings, sentient beings can be apprehended; and although there is no agent, the non-destruction of karmic fruits can be apprehended. Therefore, they are profoundly deep.

Furthermore, all dependently originated phenomena do not arise from themselves, do not arise from another, do not arise from both, nor do they arise without causes through neither self-creation nor creation by another; therefore, they are profoundly deep.

What is the meaning of "differentiation"? It refers to the differentiation of the arising of consciousness; the differentiation of internal death and birth; the differentiation of the arising of external grains and so forth; the differentiation of formation and destruction; the differentiation of sustenance by food; the differentiation of the distinction between agreeable and disagreeable destinies; the differentiation of purification; and the differentiation of majestic power—this is the meaning of differentiation.
What is meant by "in direct and reverse order"?

It refers to the direct and reverse order of defilement (*saṃkleśa*) and the direct and reverse order of purification (*vyavadāna*); this explains the meaning of the direct and reverse order of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
