In the first part, the *Vastusaṃgrahaṇī*, Chapter One, Section Three: "The Chapter on the Three Dharmas": What is conditionality (*pratyaya*)?
How many are conditions?
For what purpose is conditionality investigated?
The meaning of "condition" (pratyaya) refers to being a cause, an equal-and-immediate condition, an object-condition, and a dominant condition;
thus, all things are conditions.
One examines conditions in order to abandon the attachment to a self that is the cause of phenomena.
What are the causal conditions?
They are the ālayavijñāna and its wholesome habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Furthermore, the meaning of "causal condition" consists of: [1] essential nature, [2] differentiation, [3] accompaniment, [4] co-occurrence, [5] augmentation, [6] obstruction, and [7] appropriation.
"Self-nature" refers to the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
"Distinctions of self-nature" refers to the distinctions among efficient causes, which are briefly of twenty kinds.
The first is the "productive efficient cause," such as the conjunction of the [six] consciousnesses in relation to a consciousness.
2. The enabling cause as sustenance (*ādhāra-kāraṇa*), namely food in relation to sentient beings who have already been born or are seeking birth;
3. The enabling cause as support (*pratisthā-kāraṇa*), namely the great earth in relation to sentient beings;
4. The enabling cause as illumination (*avabhāsa-kāraṇa*), namely lamps and the like in relation to various forms.
Fifth is the efficient cause of transformation (*vipariṇāma-kāraka*), such as fire in relation to fuel.
Sixth is the efficient cause of separation (*viśleṣa-kāraka*), such as a sickle in relation to that which is being cut.
Seventh is the efficient cause of modification (*pariṇāma-kāraka*), such as technical skill in relation to gold, silver, and other materials.
8. The causal efficacy of conviction (*adhimukti-kāraka*), such as smoke in relation to fire.
9. The causal efficacy of manifestation (*abhivyakti-kāraka*), such as the thesis (*pakṣa*), reason (*hetu*), and example (*dṛṣṭānta*) in relation to the meaning to be established (*sādhyārtha*).
10. The causal efficacy of attainment (*samāpatti-kāraka*), such as the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) in relation to Nirvāṇa.
Eleventh is the efficient cause of conventional designation (*anuvyavahāra-kāraka*), which refers to names, concepts, and views.
Twelfth is the efficient cause of dependence (*apekṣā-kāraka*), which means that by depending on this, a desire for that arises; for example, depending on hunger and thirst, one seeks food and drink.
Thirteenth is the projecting efficient cause (*ākṣepaka-kāraka*), which refers to a remote condition, such as ignorance in relation to old age and death.
Fourteenth is the productive efficient cause (*abhinirvartaka-kāraka*), which refers to an immediate condition, such as ignorance in relation to formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
Fifteenth is the productive cause as appropriation (*parigraha-kāraka*), which refers to remaining conditions; for example, the field, water, and fertilizer in relation to the growth of grain.
Sixteenth is the productive cause as inducement (*āvāhaka-kāraka*), which refers to concordant conditions; for example, serving a king correctly so as to please him.

Seventeenth is the specifically determinative productive cause (*pratiniyamakāraka*), which refers to the specific condition (*viśeṣapratyaya*); for example, the conditions of the five destinies (*pañcagati*) in relation to the results of the five destinies.

Eighteenth is the cooperative productive cause (*sahakārikāraka*), which refers to the collective condition (*sāmagrīpratyaya*); for example, the non-deficiency of the sense faculties, the presence of the object, and the correct arising of attention (*manasikāra*) in relation to the consciousness that is produced.
19. Contradictory efficient cause (*viruddha-kāraka-hetu*): this refers to an obstructing condition (*vibandhaka-pratyaya*), such as hail in relation to grain.
20. Non-contradictory efficient cause (*aviruddha-kāraka-hetu*): this refers to a non-obstructing condition (*apratibandhaka-pratyaya*), such as the absence of obstacles for grain.

"Accompanying factors" (sahāya) refers to those phenomena that arise together such that none are ever lacking, as is the case, for example, with the four great elements and their derived matter, according to their respective natures.

"Co-arising factors" (sacaritra) refers to those phenomena that arise together such that their objects of perception (ālambana) are never lacking, as is the case, for example, with the mind and its mental factors (citta-caitta).

Augmentation refers to the fact that by cultivating wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate dharmas in the prior limit, one is able to cause wholesome and other such dharmas in the subsequent limit to arise in a progressively superior and increasingly refined manner.

"Obstruction" refers to the fact that, due to the repeated cultivation of various afflictions, every delusion continues to increase and become firm, thereby causing the continuum [of existence] to remain far removed from nirvāṇa.
"Appropriation" refers to unwholesome and wholesome contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), because they are able to appropriate the self-body (*ātma-bhāva*).
What is the "equal-and-immediate condition" (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?
It is so called because there is no interval between them, being equal and immediate.
The arising of mind and mental factors belonging to the same or different categories occurs because they are equal and immediate;
this is the meaning of the condition as equal and immediate antecedent (samanantara-pratyaya).
What is the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya)?

The meaning of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is defined by: having an object with limits as its focal point; having an object without limits as its focal point; having an object without diverse aspects as its focal point; having an object with diverse aspects as its focal point; having an object that is a real entity as its focal point; having an object that is not a real entity as its focal point; having an object that is a real entity as its focal point; having an object that is a conceptual construction as its focal point; having an object that is inverted as its focal point; having an object that is non-inverted as its focal point; having an obstructed object as its focal point; and having an unobstructed object as its focal point. This is the meaning of the object-condition.
What is the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*)?

It refers to the meaning of the dominant condition by way of: dominance as support, dominance as induction, dominance as coexistence, dominance as object, dominance as production, dominance as maintenance, dominance as the enjoyment of results, dominance as mundane purification and detachment from desire, and dominance as supramundane purification and detachment from desire. This is the meaning of the dominant condition.
What are the homogeneous (*sabhāga*) and the partially homogeneous (*tatsabhāga*)?
How many are homogeneous and partially homogeneous?
For what purpose are the homogeneous and partially homogeneous investigated?

This means that because those [faculties] resembling consciousness arise in a continuous stream toward their respective objects without departing from consciousness, and because they arise in a self-similar continuous stream apart from consciousness, this constitutes the meaning of "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) and "non-homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*).

A portion of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), the five [faculties] such as the eye, and a portion of the realms and bases (*dhātu-āyatana*) that possess form, are both *sabhāga* (homogeneous) and *tatsabhāga* (non-homogeneous).
One examines the homogeneous and non-homogeneous in order to abandon the attachment to a self that is either associated with or dissociated from consciousness.
What is appropriation?
How many things are appropriated?
For what purpose is appropriation investigated?
This means that because it is the physical basis for the appropriation of birth, it carries the sense of being "appropriated" (*upātta*).
A portion of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), the entirety of the five bases and elements possessing form, and a portion of four [bases] are what is appropriated.
In order to abandon attachment to a self that exercises mastery over the body, one examines the appropriated [bases].
What are the faculties?
How many are the faculties?
For what purpose are the faculties (*indriya*) examined?

They are defined as faculties because they possess predominance (*ādhipatya*) in: the apprehension of objects; the non-interruption of the lineage; the maintenance of the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*); the experience of the fruits of pure and impure karma; mundane detachment from desire; and supramundane detachment from desire. This is the meaning of "faculty."

The entire aggregate of feeling and consciousness, a portion of the aggregates of form and formations, the twelve bases and six sense fields in their entirety, and a portion of the dharma-element and dharma-base are faculties (*indriya*). One investigates the faculties in order to abandon attachment to a dominant self.
What is the nature of suffering as suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*)? How many things possess the nature of suffering as suffering?
For what purpose is the nature of suffering as suffering investigated?

This means that because of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of painful feeling itself, and because of the specific characteristic of those phenomena conducive to painful feeling, this is the meaning of the nature of suffering as suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*).
A portion of all [phenomena] constitutes the nature of suffering as suffering.
In order to abandon the attachment to a self that possesses suffering, one contemplates the nature of the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
What is the nature of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*)?
How many things constitute the nature of the suffering of change?
For what purpose is the nature of suffering as change (vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā) investigated? It means:

because the intrinsic characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of pleasant feeling is subject to change; because the intrinsic characteristic of those phenomena conducive to pleasant feeling is subject to change; and because the mind of attachment toward them is subject to change—this is the meaning of the nature of suffering as change.
All [conditioned phenomena] in part are of the nature of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*).

One examines the nature of the suffering of change in order to abandon the attachment to a self that possesses pleasure. What is the nature of the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*)?
What is the nature of suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*)? For what purpose is the nature of suffering inherent in conditioned formations investigated?

It is because of the specific characteristic of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*aduḥkhāsukha-vedanā*); because of the specific characteristic of those phenomena that accord with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; because of being gripped by the heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) of both [painful and pleasant feelings]; and because of the lack of security due to the persistence of impermanence within both. This is the meaning of the nature of suffering inherent in conditioned formations.
Excluding one portion of the aggregates within the three realms and two bases, all else is of the nature of suffering as conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
One examines the nature of suffering as conditioned formations in order to relinquish attachment to a self that is neither painful nor pleasant.
What is that which possesses maturation?
How many possess maturation?
For what purpose is that which possesses maturation investigated?
That which is unwholesome and that which is wholesome yet tainted (*sāsrava*) possesses maturation (*savipāka*).
Ten elements (*dhātu*), four bases (*āyatana*), and a portion of the aggregates (*skandha*) possess maturation.
One examines what possesses maturation in order to abandon the attachment to a self that is capable of relinquishing and continuing the aggregates.

Furthermore, as for "maturation" (*vipāka*), it refers exclusively to the *ālayavijñāna* and its associated mental factors; all others are merely "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*) but are not themselves "maturation.
What is nutriment?
How many are nutriments?
For what purpose is nutriment investigated?

It is because of transformation; because that which undergoes transformation has an object; because that which has an object has aspiration; and because that which has aspiration has grasping—this is the meaning of nutriment.
Three aggregates, eleven elements, and a portion of five bases constitute nutriment.
One examines nutriment in order to abandon attachment to a self that subsists by means of nutriment.
Furthermore, when established according to its distinctions, this nutriment is briefly of four kinds:

First, subsisting on food based on the impure; second, subsisting on food based on both the pure and the impure; third, subsisting on food based on the completely pure; fourth, subsisting on food through manifestation.
What is "having a superior"?
How many things have a superior?
For what purpose is that which has a superior investigated?
This means that because they consist of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) and a portion of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), they possess the quality of being "surpassable" (*sottara*).
With the exception of a portion of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) and the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*), everything else is surpassable.
In order to abandon attachment to a self that clings to inferior things, one contemplates that which is surpassable.
What is unsurpassable?
How many are unsurpassable?
For what reason is it observed as "unsurpassed"?
Because it is a portion of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), this is the meaning of "unsurpassed.
A portion of the *dharmadhātu* and the *dharmāyatana* is unsurpassed.
In order to abandon attachment to a self that is supreme among things, one investigates the unsurpassed.
By means of the principles of differentiation explained here, other immeasurable modes of investigation may be understood by analogy.

Furthermore, there are briefly three types of distinctions among the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases: namely, the distinction of the characteristics of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-lakṣaṇa), the distinction of the characteristics of the discriminated (vikalpita-lakṣaṇa), and the distinction of the characteristics of the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā-lakṣaṇa).
What are the distinctions of the characteristics of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva)?
They refer to the self, sentient being, life-force, creature, nourisher, person, mind-born, and manava, which are thoroughly imagined within the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
What is the differentiation of the characteristics of the objects of conceptualization?
It refers to the phenomena of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
What is the differentiation of the characteristics of the nature of phenomena?
This refers to the absence of a self-nature (*ātman*) and the presence of a selflessness (*anātman*) within the very aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*).

Furthermore, there are four kinds of distinctions: the distinction of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the distinction of conceptualization (*vikalpa*), the distinction of basis (*niśraya*), and the distinction of continuity (*saṃtati*).
What is the differentiation of characteristics?
It refers to the differentiation of the individual characteristics of each of the aggregates, elements, and bases.
What is the differentiation of conceptualization?

That is to say, within the very aggregates, elements, and bases, there are distinctions such as those that exist substantially and those that exist nominally; those that exist conventionally and those that exist ultimately; those that are with form and those that are formless; those that are visible and those that are invisible—and thus there are immeasurable such distinctions and classifications, as previously explained.
What is the distinction of the basis?
It should be understood that as far as there are distinctions of the bases for sentient beings, so too are there [distinctions] of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields.
What is the distinction of the continuity?
That is to say, regarding the transformation of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases in each and every moment:
what is to be understood through skill in the differentiation of their characteristics?
It is the understanding of the faults of the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*).
What is understood through skill in the differentiation of conceptualization?
It is the understanding of the faults associated with the perception of a collection (*piṇḍasaṃjñā*).
What is understood through skill in the differentiation of the basis (*āśraya*)?
This refers to understanding the faults of the notion that [results] are obtained without acting and lost despite acting.
What is understood through skill in the distinctions of the mental continuum?
It refers to understanding the faults of the notion of abiding.

Furthermore, there are six types of distinctions regarding the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases: namely, the distinction of the external door, the distinction of the internal door, the distinction of long duration, the distinction of limited duration, the distinction of momentary duration, and the distinction of manifestation.
What is the distinction of the outward-directed gate?
It refers mostly to the distinctions of the desire realm.
What is the distinction of the inward-directed gate?
This refers to all stages of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*).
What is the distinction regarding duration?
It refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
What is the distinction of temporal limits?
It refers to all those in training (*śaikṣa*), as well as those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) with the exception of the final moment of the aggregates, elements, and bases.
What is the distinction of duration?
This refers to the aggregates, elements, and bases at the final moment of all those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
What is the distinction that is manifested?
It refers to the aggregates, elements, and bases manifested by the Buddhas and the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have attained ultimate perfection.
2. Chapter on Compendium (*Saṃgrahapaṭala*). In the second chapter, the Compendium, within the *Mūlavastu* of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, it is asked: What is compendium?

Briefly stated, there are eleven kinds of compendium: namely, compendium by characteristic (*lakṣaṇasaṃgraha*), compendium by realm (*dhātusaṃgraha*), compendium by category (*jātisaṃgraha*), compendium by state (*avasthāsaṃgraha*), compendium by accompaniment (*sahāyasaṃgraha*), compendium by direction (*deśasaṃgraha*), compendium by time (*kālasaṃgraha*), compendium by one part (*ekadeśasaṃgraha*), compendium by the whole (*sakalasaṃgraha*), compendium by mutual inclusion (*anyonyasaṃgraha*), and compendium by ultimate meaning (*paramārthasaṃgraha*).
What is inclusion by way of characteristics?
It means that the individual self-characteristics of each of the aggregates, elements, and bases include themselves by their very nature.
What is inclusion by way of elements?
This means that the *ālayavijñāna*, which contains all the seeds of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*), is able to subsume those realms.
In what manner does it subsume them?
Although the characteristics of the aggregates, elements, and bases differ, they are mutually subsumed because they share the same essential meaning of "aggregate," "element," and "base."
What is inclusion by way of state (*avasthā*)?
It means that the aggregates, elements, and bases in a state of pleasure are included by their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
The same applies to states of suffering and states of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure, because these states are equivalent.
What is inclusion by way of association?

It means that because the aggregate of form and the other aggregates are mutually associated, they include one another as assisting companions; the same applies to the other aggregates, elements, and bases.
What is inclusion by way of direction?
This means that the aggregates, elements, and bases of the eastern direction mutually subsume one another; the same applies to the aggregates, elements, and bases of the other directions.
As for what constitutes temporal inclusion:
the aggregates, elements, and bases of the past mutually subsume one another, and the same applies to those of the future and the present.
What is inclusion by a single part?
It refers to those phenomena included within the aggregates, elements, and bases that are included as only one part and not the remainder; this should be understood as inclusion by a single part.
What is inclusion by the whole?
It should be understood that all phenomena (dharmas) comprised within and comprising the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and bases (āyatana) are included in their entirety.
What is mutual inclusion?
Specifically, how many elements and how many bases are included within the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha)?
One part of the ten [aggregates].
How many elements and how many bases are subsumed under the aggregate of feeling? One part.
As it is with the aggregate of feeling, so it is with the aggregates of perception and mental formations.
How many elements and how many bases are subsumed within the aggregate of consciousness?
Seven elements and one base.
How many aggregates (*skandha*) and how many bases (*āyatana*) are subsumed under the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*)?
A portion of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and one entire base [the eye-base].
As it is with the eye-element, so it is with the elements of ear, nose, tongue, body, visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects.
How many aggregates and how many bases are subsumed under the mind-element (*manodhātu*)?
One aggregate and one base.
How many aggregates and how many bases are subsumed under the phenomena-element (*dharmadhātu*)?
The three aggregates in their entirety, a portion of the aggregate of form, and one base in its entirety are subsumed under the eye-consciousness element.
How many aggregates and how many bases are subsumed under the consciousness element?
A portion of the aggregate of consciousness and a portion of the mind base.
As it is with the eye-consciousness element, so it is with the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness elements.
How many aggregates and how many elements are subsumed within the eye-base?
A portion of the aggregate of form and one entire element.
As it is with the sense base of the eye, so it is with the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
How many aggregates and how many elements are subsumed within the sense base of the mind?
One aggregate and seven elements.
How many aggregates (*skandha*), how many elements (*dhātu*), and how many bases (*āyatana*) are included within the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*)?
It includes three aggregates in their entirety, a portion of one [aggregate], and one element in its entirety.

In this manner, all other phenomena—whether designated by the names of aggregates, elements, and bases, or designated by names other than aggregates, elements, and bases; whether they exist substantially (*dravyasat*), nominally (*prajñaptisat*), conventionally (*saṃvṛtisat*), or ultimately (*paramārthasat*); whether they are objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), objects of cognition (*vijñeya*), or objects of realization (*adhigamya*); whether they are material (*rūpin*) or immaterial (*arūpin*), visible (*sanidarśana*) or invisible (*anidarśana*)—should be understood, as previously elucidated, to be fully subsumed within the aggregates, elements, and bases according to their respective correspondences.
What is inclusion by way of the ultimate truth?
It refers to being included within the suchness (*tathatā*) of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
What benefit is obtained through skill in this inclusion?
One attains the benefit of brief synthesis regarding the objects of focus (*ālambana*).
As one briefly gathers the mind upon various respective objects, so too do the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*) increase and become superior.
Chapter Three: The Chapter on Association (*Saṃprayoga*) from the *Mūlavastu* of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*. What is association?

Briefly stated, there are six kinds of association (*samyoga*): namely, inseparable association, combined association, accumulated association, coexistent association, functional association, and associated association.
What is inseparable association?
It refers to all material forms possessing spatial dimensions being mutually inseparable from the location of the atom (*paramāṇu*).
What is combined association?
This refers to all material forms possessing spatial dimensions that are above the level of the atom, which mutually combine.
What is meant by "aggregation and conjunction"?
It refers to the successive gathering together of material forms with spatial dimensions.
What is concomitance by coexistence (*sahabhū-saṃprayoga*)?
It refers to the aggregates, elements, and bases within a single body that evolve simultaneously, arising, abiding, and ceasing together.
What is concomitance by function (*kāritra-saṃprayoga*)?
This refers to mutual inclusion regarding a single task to be performed, such as two bhikṣus who correspond with one another in accordance with a single activity.
What is "correspondence through common practice"?
This refers to the mind and mental factors acting in concert toward a single object.

This association of concerted action has further meanings: namely, association with that which is of another nature rather than one's own nature; association with that which is non-contradictory rather than contradictory; association at the same time rather than at different times; and association within the same sphere and stage rather than different spheres and stages.
Furthermore, there is the universal association of concomitant factors, namely:
feeling, perception, volition, contact, and mental consciousness.
Furthermore, there is the defiled universal association of concomitant factors, namely: the four types of afflictions within the defiled mind.

Furthermore, there are those that do not function in association at all times; namely, the mind upon which they depend, which at times gives rise to virtuous states such as faith, and at other times gives rise to afflictions and secondary afflictions such as greed.

Furthermore, there is association by way of state and common activity, namely: the various associated dharmas with pleasant feeling, and the various associated dharmas with painful feeling and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Furthermore, there is uninterrupted concomitance of similar activity (*sahabhū-saṃprayoga*), which refers to the state of having a mind (*sacittaka-avasthā*).
Furthermore, there is interrupted concomitance of similar activity, which refers to being separated by mindless absorptions (*acittaka-samāpatti*).
Furthermore, there is external-door association by way of commonality, which refers mostly to the minds and mental factors bound to the desire realm.
Furthermore, there is internal-door association by way of commonality, which refers to all the minds and mental factors belonging to the stages of meditative concentration (*samāhita-bhūmi*).

Furthermore, there is association with that which has been previously practiced and accompanied by commonality, namely, all the minds and mental factors of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), as well as a portion of the minds and mental factors of those in training (*śaikṣa*).

Furthermore, there is association with that which has not been previously practiced and lacks commonality, namely, all supramundane (*lokottara*) minds and mental factors, as well as the minds and mental factors subsequently attained after emerging from the supramundane state during its initial and final stages.
What benefit is gained from skill in association?

One is able to thoroughly understand the meaning of the association and non-association of all phenomena—such as sensation and perception, whether defiled or purified—which depend solely upon the mind.

Through this realization, one is able to abandon the attachment to a self that perceives itself as the agent of feeling, perceiving, intending, and remembering, as well as the attachment to defilement and purity; furthermore, one can skillfully and swiftly enter into the state of non-self.
Chapter Four: On Attainment (*Prāpti*) In the fourth chapter, "On Attainment," within the *Mūlavastu* of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, it is asked: What is attainment?
It refers to the characteristics of attainment as previously described.
This differentiation is threefold: namely, the accomplishment of seeds, the accomplishment of mastery, and the accomplishment of manifest activity.
What is the accomplishment of seeds?
That is to say, if one is born in the desire realm, one possesses the afflictions and secondary afflictions associated with the desire, form, and formless realms by virtue of possessing their seeds;
as well as the innate wholesome states.

If one is born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one possesses the afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) by virtue of possessing their seeds;

yet they are also said to be non-existent [in manifest form]. One likewise possesses the afflictions and secondary afflictions bound to the form and formless realms by virtue of possessing their seeds, as well as the innate wholesome states (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*).

If one is born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), one possesses the afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) bound to the desire and form realms by virtue of possessing their seeds;

yet they are also said to be "not possessed" [in their manifest form]. Furthermore, one possesses the afflictions and secondary afflictions bound to the formless realm by virtue of possessing their seeds, as well as innate wholesomeness (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*).

If one has already attained the path that serves as the antidote to the three realms, then as each specific category of antidote arises, the corresponding category [of afflictions] ceases to be established by way of its seeds and becomes non-established.

In whatever manner and according to whichever category of antidotes has not yet arisen, in that very manner and according to that very category, [the seeds] are accomplished by virtue of being established as seeds.
What is accomplishment through mastery?

This refers to all wholesome dharmas of application, as well as mundane and supramundane qualities such as dhyāna, vimokṣa, samādhi, and samāpatti, along with a portion of indeterminate dharmas; these are accomplished by way of the accomplishment of mastery.
What is accomplishment by way of manifestation?
It refers to the phenomena of the aggregates, elements, and bases as they manifest before one—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate—which are accomplished by virtue of that manifestation.
If one has already severed the roots of goodness, all wholesome dharmas are "accomplished" by virtue of being established as seeds;
yet they are also termed "unaccomplished. Furthermore, those of the *icchantika* type who lack the nature for *nirvāṇa* ultimately accomplish all defiled dharmas.

One is also called an *ātyantika* (one who is ultimately incapable) due to the absence of the causes for liberation, because the attainment of the cause for that liberation will never be accomplished.
What benefit is gained by achieving skill in this accomplishment?
One is able to thoroughly understand the increase and decrease of all phenomena.
Because of this knowledge of increase and decrease, one abandons the notion of certainty regarding the rise and fall of the world, and is even able to sever both craving and aversion.
2. Section on Ascertainment (Viniścaya-vibhāga), Chapter 1: On the Truths (Satya-paṭala). Part 1 of the First Chapter of the *Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccaya-viniścaya*. What is ascertainment?

Briefly stated, there are four kinds of definitive analysis (viniścaya): namely, definitive analysis of the truths (satya-viniścaya), definitive analysis of phenomena (dharma-viniścaya), definitive analysis of attainment (prāpti-viniścaya), and definitive analysis of discussion (saṃkathya-viniścaya).
What is the definitive analysis of the truths?
They are the Four Noble Truths: the truth of suffering, the truth of the origin, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path.
What is the truth of suffering?
It refers to the birth of sentient beings and the basis upon which they are born.
What are sentient beings who are born?
This refers to the world of sentient beings;
that is, all sentient beings who are born within the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas.
These are known as Pūrvavideha in the east, Aparagoyānī in the west, Jambudvīpa in the south, and Uttarakuru in the north.

The gods are as follows: the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; the Brahmakāyika Heaven, the Brahmapurohita Heaven, the Mahābrahmā Heaven, the Parīttābha Heaven, the Apramāṇābha Heaven, the Ābhāsvara Heaven, the Parīttaśubha Heaven, the Apramāṇaśubha Heaven, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, the Anabhraka Heaven, the Puṇyaprasava Heaven, the Bṛhatphala Heaven, the Avṛha Heaven, the Atapa Heaven, the Sudṛśa Heaven, the Sudarśana Heaven, and the Akaniṣṭha Heaven; as well as the Heaven of Infinite Space, the Heaven of Infinite Consciousness, the Heaven of Nothingness, and the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception.
What is the locus upon which birth depends?
It is the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).
That is to say, the water-circle rests upon the wind-circle, and the earth-circle rests upon the water-circle.
Resting upon this earth-wheel are Mount Sumeru, the seven golden mountain ranges, the four great continents, the eight intermediate islands, the inner ocean, and the outer ocean.
Beyond the four tiers surrounding Mount Sumeru are the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
The abodes of the Trāyastriṃśa gods are distinct, consisting of the outer Cakravāḍa mountains and palaces in the sky.
So too are the distinct abodes of the Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods, as well as those of the gods of the Form Realm (rūpadhātu).
There are distinct abodes for the various asuras, as well as distinct abodes for the various hell-beings (nāraka), namely: the hot hells, the cold hells, and the solitary hells.

Including the distinct abodes of certain animals and hungry ghosts, and extending as far as the regions illuminated by the pervasive radiance of one sun and one moon, is called a single world-system (*lokadhātu*).

Within such a thousandfold world-system, there are a thousand suns, a thousand moons, a thousand Sumeru Kings of Mountains, a thousand sets of four great continents, a thousand Cāturmahārājakāyika heavens, a thousand Trāyastriṃśa heavens, a thousand Yāma heavens, a thousand Tuṣita heavens, a thousand Nirmāṇarati heavens, a thousand Paranirmitavaśavartin heavens, and a thousand Brahmakāyika heavens; this total is collectively termed a small thousandfold world-system (*sāhasracūdika lokadhātu*).
One thousand small chiliocosms are collectively termed a second-order medium chiliocosm; one thousand medium chiliocosms are collectively termed a third-order great trichiliocosm.
Such a great trichiliocosm is entirely encircled by a Great Cakravāḍa mountain range.
Furthermore, this trichiliocosm is destroyed and formed simultaneously.

It is like rain falling from the sky in drops as thick as axle-trees, pouring down without interval or interruption; likewise, in the eastern direction, there are immeasurable worlds without interval or interruption, some about to be destroyed, some about to be formed, some currently being destroyed, some remaining after destruction, some currently being formed, or remaining after formation.
As it is in the eastern direction, so it is likewise in all the ten directions.

Whether the world of sentient beings or the receptacle world, because they are produced by the power of karma and afflictions, and arise through the predominance of karma and afflictions, they are collectively termed the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).

Furthermore, there are pure worlds that are not subsumed under the truth of suffering, because they are not produced by the power of karma and afflictions, nor are they arisen through the predominance of karma and afflictions; rather, they are induced by the predominance of pure roots of goodness resulting from great vows.
The place where this is produced is inconceivable and is realized only by a Buddha;
it is not even within the meditative range of those who have attained dhyāna, let alone within the reach of mere intellectual speculation.

Furthermore, there are eight specific varieties of the characteristic of suffering: namely, the suffering of birth, the suffering of aging, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of association with the disliked, the suffering of separation from the beloved, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and, in brief, the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging.
For what reason is birth suffering?
Because it is oppressed by manifold sufferings and because it is the basis for other sufferings.
For what reason is old age suffering?
Because of the suffering of transformation over time;
why is illness suffering?
Because of the suffering of the transformation of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Why is death suffering?
Because it is the suffering of the transformation and decay of the life-force one has received.
Why is association with the disliked suffering?
Because the meeting [of what is loved] gives rise to suffering.
Why is separation from what is loved suffering?
Because separation gives rise to suffering.
Why is the failure to obtain what one seeks suffering?
Because the non-fulfillment of one's hopes gives rise to suffering.
Why is the brief summary of all five aggregates of clinging suffering?
Because of the suffering of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).

These eight kinds [of suffering] are briefly subsumed into six: namely, the suffering of oppression, the suffering of transformation, the suffering of association, the suffering of separation, the suffering of not obtaining what is desired, and the suffering of coarse heaviness.
Thus, these six types are extensively expanded into eight; whether six or eight, they are equal and identical.
As it is said regarding the three types of suffering, among these eight types of suffering, do the three encompass the eight, or do the eight encompass the three?
They are mutually inclusive, as follows:

the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, and the suffering of association with the disliked manifest the nature of suffering-as-suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*);
the suffering of separation from the beloved and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks manifest the nature of change-as-suffering (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).
Briefly summarized, all suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) can manifest the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*).
As it is said, there are two types of suffering: namely, suffering according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) and suffering according to ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
What is suffering according to conventional truth?
What is suffering according to ultimate truth?
That which ranges from the suffering of birth to the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks is suffering according to conventional truth.
Briefly summarized, all suffering of the five aggregates of clinging is the suffering of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
What is the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the Truth of Suffering?
It is the characteristic of impermanence, the characteristic of suffering, the characteristic of emptiness, and the characteristic of non-self.
What are the characteristics of impermanence?

Briefly, there are twelve: namely, the characteristic of non-existence, the characteristic of destruction, the characteristic of transformation, the characteristic of separation, the characteristic of manifestation, the characteristic of natural law, the characteristic of momentariness, the characteristic of continuity, the characteristic of illness and so forth, the characteristic of the shifting of various mental activities, the characteristic of the rise and fall of assets, and the characteristic of the formation and disintegration of the receptacle world.
What is the characteristic of non-existence?
It refers to the fact that at all times, the nature of "self" and "mine" is eternally non-existent within the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
What is the characteristic of disintegration?
This means that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), having arisen, immediately perish, for they exist only momentarily before returning to non-existence.
What is the characteristic of transformation?
It means that conditioned phenomena arise differently, because they proceed through a succession of dissimilar states.
What is the characteristic of separation?
It refers to the loss of sovereign power over conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), or their being appropriated by another as their own possession.
What is the characteristic of presence?
This refers to present impermanence, which arises because one currently undergoes impermanence due to being pursued by its causes.
What is the characteristic of natural law (*dharmatā*)?
It refers to future impermanence, which arises because one will certainly undergo it due to being pursued by its causes.
What is the characteristic of the moment?
It refers to the moments of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), because they necessarily do not persist beyond that moment.
What is the characteristic of continuity?
This refers to the fact that, from beginningless time, the arising and ceasing of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) continues in an uninterrupted succession.
What are the characteristics of illness and so forth?
They refer to the transformations of the four great elements, the seasons, and the life-force.
What is the characteristic of the various modes of mental activity?

It refers to the fact that at one time a mind associated with greed arises, and at another time a mind free from greed arises; likewise, there are minds with hatred and free from hatred, with delusion and free from delusion, conjoined or dispersed, depressed or uplifted, agitated or free from agitation, unpeaceful or peaceful, concentrated or unconcentrated—because the mind flows and turns in such modes of activity.
What are the signs of the rise and fall of material assets?
It refers to the fact that all flourishing virtues ultimately end in decline and transformation.
What are the signs of the formation and destruction of the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*)?
This refers to the three types of destruction by fire, water, and wind, which bring about the formation and disintegration [of worlds]. The "summits" refer to the second, third, and fourth dhyānas.

Although the external palaces and so forth of the fourth dhyāna do not undergo formation and disintegration through external calamities, it is said that they undergo formation and disintegration because those devas and their palaces arise and perish together.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of intermediate kalpas, namely those of famine, pestilence, and warfare.
These three minor calamities appear only at the final stage of a kalpa.

That is to say, once the world has been formed, during the first intermediate kalpa there is only decrease, and during the final intermediate kalpa there is only increase; eighteen intermediate kalpas involve both increase and decrease; twenty intermediate kalpas are for the world’s actual destruction; twenty intermediate kalpas are for the world to remain after it has been destroyed; twenty intermediate kalpas are for the world’s actual formation; and twenty intermediate kalpas are for the world to remain after it has been formed.

Combining these eighty intermediate kalpas constitutes one great kalpa (*mahākalpa*). By means of this reckoning of kalpas, the lifespans of the various devas in the form and formless realms are revealed; as it is said, "due to the exhaustion of lifespan, the exhaustion of merit, and the exhaustion of karma, those respective sentient beings pass away from their respective abodes."
What is the exhaustion of lifespan?
It refers to death at the [natural] time.
What is the exhaustion of merit?
This refers to untimely death, which is death due to the exhaustion of merit.
Because those sentient beings are attached to the flavor of meditative absorption, their power of merit is completely depleted, and they consequently meet their end.
What is meant by the exhaustion of karma?

This refers to dying because both *upapadya-vedanīya* karma (karma to be experienced in the next life) and *aparaparyāya-vedanīya* karma (karma to be experienced in subsequent lives) have been exhausted.
What are the characteristics of suffering?
They are either the three types of suffering, the eight types of suffering, or the six types of suffering, as explained in detail previously; these are called the characteristics of suffering.
For what reason does the Sūtra state that "whatever is impermanent is suffering"?
It is because the characteristic of suffering can be discerned by virtue of two aspects of impermanence acting as conditions.
That is to say, by virtue of the aspect of impermanence in arising, the nature of the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) can be discerned; and...
The nature of suffering as destruction (vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā) can be understood by taking the impermanence of cessation as its condition;
the nature of suffering as conditioned formations (saṃskāraduḥkhatā) can be understood by taking the impermanence of both [arising and cessation] as its condition.
Based on this very meaning, the Blessed One said:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; all conditioned phenomena are subject to decay.
Furthermore, based on this same meaning, he said: "Whatever is felt, I declare that to be suffering."

Furthermore, because the eight types of suffering, such as birth and so forth, are present within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that follow upon the two dharmas of arising and ceasing, and because their nature can be clearly understood, the Buddha said:
"That which is impermanent is suffering."
Furthermore, regarding the fact that suffering such as birth can be discerned within impermanent conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), the Tathāgata spoke with this underlying intention (*abhiprāya*):
"Because they are impermanent, they are suffering," but he did not say this of all conditioned phenomena.
What is the characteristic of emptiness?
It is that when something is not present in a particular place, one correctly contemplates that place as empty by virtue of that principle;
and when something else remains present in that place, one knows it as it truly is, as being present by virtue of that principle—this is called skillfully entering into emptiness.
To know things as they truly are means to be free from inversion.
In what respect and for whom does non-existence apply?
Within the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, there is no self, no "mine," and so forth—no phenomena that are permanent, eternal, stable, abiding, or immutable.
By this reasoning, all those things are empty.
Wherein could there be anything else?
In that very place, there is the nature of selflessness.
This absence of self-nature in the "self" and the presence of selflessness is called emptiness.
Therefore, the Blessed One spoke with intentional meaning:
"That which exists, know it as it truly exists; that which does not exist, know it as it truly does not exist."

Furthermore, there are three kinds of emptiness: the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of suchness (*tathatā-śūnyatā*), and the emptiness of reality (*bhūtatā-śūnyatā*).

The first is based on the observation of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); the second is based on the observation of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); and the third is based on the observation of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
What is the characteristic of selflessness?

It refers to the fact that the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases do not possess the characteristics of a self as established by those who propound a theory of self; because the characteristics of a self do not exist within the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, they are called the characteristic of selflessness.
Therefore, the Bhagavat spoke with intentional meaning, saying:
"All phenomena are without self.
As the World-Honored One said:
"All this is not mine; this is not my abode; this is not my self.
Regarding such a meaning, one should observe it as it truly is with right wisdom.
What is the meaning of this statement?

It means that regarding external phenomena, it was spoken with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*) that "all this is not mine"; and regarding internal phenomena, it was spoken with intentional meaning that "this is not my self" and "in this there is no self."
Why is this so? Because regarding external phenomena, one conceives of them solely as "mine" (mamakāra); therefore, one merely eliminates "mine.
Regarding internal phenomena, one conceives of them both as "self" (ātman) and "mine"; therefore, one eliminates both "self" and "mine."
It was previously stated that all impermanent things possess the characteristic of momentariness; how is this known?

Just as the mind and mental factors possess the characteristic of momentariness, one should know that form and the other aggregates likewise possess the characteristic of momentariness, because they are appropriated by the mind, because their well-being and peril are equal to those of the mind, because they undergo transformation in accordance with the mind, because they are the support of the mind, because they arise through the predominance of the mind, and because they function under the sovereignty of the mind.

Furthermore, because transformation and decay can be observed in its final stage, and because it perishes naturally without depending on external conditions once it has arisen, one should contemplate that form and the other aggregates likewise perish moment by moment.
As the Blessed One has said:
"Whatever forms there are, all of them are either the four great elements or derived from the four great elements.
With what intention was this said?
Based on the possibility [of such a designation], it may be said that they exist in the same location; based on this [existence], there is the meaning of "being produced.
If a particular primary element (*mahābhūta*) is obtainable within a given aggregate, one should know that this aggregate contains only that primary element and no others.
In some aggregates there is only one primary element (mahābhūta), in some two, and in others even all of them; the same applies to the derived matter (upādāyarūpa).
If a certain derived matter is found within a particular aggregate, it should be known that this aggregate consists of that alone and nothing else.
There may be an aggregate consisting of only one derived form (*upādāya-rūpa*), or two derived forms, or even many derived forms, according to what is appropriate.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that gross aggregates of matter are composed of a collection of atoms (*paramāṇu*), it should be understood that in this context the atom has no substantial reality; rather, it is established as an "atom" by means of the analytical intellect gradually breaking down and reducing matter until the limit of divisibility is reached, and it is in reference to this limit that the atom is posited.
This is for the purpose of dispelling the notion of a unified whole and for the purpose of realizing that all forms (*rūpa*) are not truly real.

Furthermore, there are briefly eight types of distinctions regarding the nature of suffering (*duḥkha*): namely, extensive non-quiescent suffering; quiescent suffering; suffering that is both quiescent and non-quiescent; middling non-quiescent suffering; subtle non-quiescent suffering; subtle quiescent suffering; extremely subtle quiescent suffering; and that which is not suffering but resembles suffering while abiding in great quiescence.
What is the vast and non-quiescent suffering?
It refers to those born in the desire realm who have never accumulated any roots of goodness.
What is quiescent suffering?
This refers to those who have already produced the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).
What is suffering that is both tranquil and non-tranquil?
It refers to those who, having already produced roots of goodness by means of the worldly path (*laukikamārga*) to become free from desire.
What is the suffering of middling non-quiescence?
It refers to those born in the form realm who have distanced themselves from the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).
What is the suffering of slight non-quiescence?
This refers to those born in the formless realm who have distanced themselves from the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).
What is subtle, slight, and tranquil suffering?
It refers to those who are still in training (*śaikṣa*).
What is the extremely subtle, tranquil suffering?
It refers to the six sense bases which serve as the conditions for the persistence of the life-faculty of those beyond training (aśaikṣas).
What is that which is not suffering but resembles suffering while abiding in great tranquility?
This refers to Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have already attained the ultimate goal, yet take birth within the various realms of existence by virtue of the power of their great compassion and vows.
Furthermore, the suffering of death was previously explained.
There are three kinds of death: namely, death with a wholesome mind, death with an unwholesome mind, or death with a neutral mind. Regarding death with a wholesome mind:

this refers to the state in which a clear and sharp mind is active; either sustained by the power of one's own roots of virtue, or induced by another, one gives rise to a wholesome mind as one approaches the point of death.

Death with an unwholesome mind refers to the state of passing away while an unwholesome mind arises, occurring either because one is sustained by the power of one's own unwholesome roots or because one is led astray by others, even while in a state where a clear and sharp mind is active.

Death with an indeterminate mind refers to when one approaches the state of finality of life while an indeterminate mind is active—whether in a state where a sharp and clear mind is functioning, or in a state where a dull and unclear mind is functioning, or due to the absence of two conditions, or due to the lack of efficacy in preparatory effort.
For one who practices pure conduct, at the moment of death, the sensation of cold first arises in the lower part of the body.
For one who practices impure conduct, at the moment of death, the sensation of cold first arises in the upper part of the body.
When one who has practiced impure conduct is born into the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), its appearance manifests like the light of a black lamb or like the darkness of a cloudy night.
When one who has practiced pure conduct is born into the intermediate state, its appearance manifests like the light of white silk or like a clear night.

Furthermore, this intermediate state (*antarābhava*) exists at the moment of taking birth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), as well as following the end of life in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); it is also termed "mind-born" (*manomaya*) and "gandharva," and so forth.
It remains for at most seven days, though it may perish prematurely or transition at any time.

While abiding in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one is also capable of accumulating various karmas, because wholesome and other volitions (*cetanā*) induced by the force of prior habitual practice manifest.
Furthermore, one can see sentient beings of a similar class.
Moreover, the form of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) resembles that of the place where one is to be born.

Additionally, within this state, there is no obstruction regarding the destination; like one possessing supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), one comes and goes with great speed, yet one still encounters physical constraints at the place of birth.

Furthermore, regarding this intermediate state (*antarābhava*), the process of its final disappearance and the moment of linking to a new birth at the place of rebirth follow the principle of the rising and falling of the two ends of a scale.
While abiding in the intermediate state, one generates craving for the place of rebirth, with other afflictions (*kleśa*) serving as auxiliary conditions.
In this state, the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) ceases together with craving, and the *kalala* body arises together with consciousness; this is exclusively maturation (*vipāka*).
From this point onward, the faculties gradually develop, as described in the section on dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Among the four types of birth, one may undergo birth from an egg, or birth from a womb, or birth from moisture, or miraculous birth.
