Section One on Determination: Chapter One on the Truths, Part Three. What is the truth of cessation?

The truth of cessation is analyzed by way of its characteristics, its profundity, the conventional, the ultimate, the incomplete, the complete, the unadorned, the adorned, that which has a remainder, that which has no remainder, the most excellent, and its distinctions.
By what characteristics?

That is to say, the non-arising of afflictions through true suchness and the noble path—whether as the basis for cessation, that which effects cessation, or the nature of cessation—is the characteristic of the truth of cessation.
As the Blessed One said:
"The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—in this place, name-and-form (nāmarūpa) are extinguished without remainder.
He further said:

Therefore, you should now contemplate this state: namely, that in this state the eye is ultimately extinguished and detached from the perception of forms, and so on, until the mind is ultimately extinguished and detached from the perception of phenomena.

By this principle, it is shown that the cessation of contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) within the objective sphere of suchness (*tathatā*) as the focal object is the characteristic of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). Why is it profound?

It is because those conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) are ultimately quiescent; and this quiescence, in relation to those formations, cannot be said to be different, nor can it be said not to be different, nor can it be said to be both different and not different, nor can it be said to be neither different nor not different.
Why is this? Because it is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Within this meaning, if one were to give rise to conceptual proliferation, it would not be correct reflection, nor the Path, nor reality (*tathatā*), nor skillful means of reflection.
As the Blessed One has said:
"The exhaustion of these six bases of contact, their freedom from desire, their cessation, their stilling, and their disappearance.

To say they are different, or that they are not different, or that they are both different and not different, or that they are neither different nor not different—this is to produce conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) where there is no proliferation; for as long as the six sense bases exist, there can be such conceptual proliferations.
When the six sense bases have ceased and all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) are extinguished, that is *nirvāṇa*.
Why is it called "conventional"?
It refers to the cessation obtained by suppressing the seeds through the mundane path; for this reason, the Blessed One designated it by the specific name "partial *nirvāṇa*" (*tad-aṃśika-nirvāṇa*).
What is meant by "in terms of the ultimate"?
It refers to the cessation attained by permanently uprooting the seeds through noble wisdom.
What is meant by "in terms of being incomplete"?

This refers to all cessations belonging to those in training (*śaikṣa*), whether they are comprised within the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*), or the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmi-phala*).
In what sense is it "complete"?
This refers to all cessations included within the fruit of arhatship for those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Why is it called "unadorned"?
It refers to the cessation belonging to arhats who are liberated through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta*).
In what sense is it "endowed with adornment"?
It refers to the cessation belonging to Arhats who are liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*) and possess the three knowledges (*trividyā*) and six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
In what sense is it "with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*)?
This refers to the cessation with remainder.
What is the cessation without remainder?
It refers to the cessation without remainder.
What is it that makes it supreme?
It refers to the cessation encompassed by the non-abiding nirvāṇa of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, because they dwell eternally in the performance of the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings.
What is the distinction?

It refers to such terms as "without remainder," "permanent abandonment," "permanent emergence," "permanent vomiting out," "exhaustion," "detachment from desire," "cessation," "tranquility," and "disappearance."
Why is it called "perpetual abandonment without remainder"?
It is because of the subsequent phrases.
Why is it called "eternal emergence"?
Because it forever brings about the emergence from all fetters.
Why is it called "forever disgorging"?
Because it forever disgorges the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Why is it called "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*)?
Because one attains dissociation (*visamyoga*) through the antidotes of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Why is it called "detachment from desire" (*vairāgya*)?
Because one attains dissociation through the counteractive measures of the path of cultivation,
why is it called "cessation"?
Because the suffering that constitutes its future fruit does not arise.
Why is it called "tranquility"?
Because in this present life, the mental suffering that constitutes its fruit never again arises.
Why is it called "subsidence"?
Because all other phenomena have forever ceased and vanished.
Why is this cessation further called "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*)?
Because it is free from the three characteristics [of arising, abiding, and ceasing].
For what reason is this cessation further called "difficult to see"?
Because it transcends the domain of both the fleshly eye and the divine eye.
For what reason is this cessation further called "non-reverting"?
Because it is forever free from the differentiated transitions of the various realms of existence.
For what reason is this cessation called "non-humiliation"?
Because it is free from the three types of craving.
For what reason is this cessation further named "ambrosia"?
Because it is free from the demon of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*).
For what reason is this cessation further named "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*)?
Because it is forever free from all affliction-māras.
For what reason is this cessation further called a "dwelling"?
Because it is the basis for faultless joy and bliss.
For what reason is this cessation further named an "island"?
Because the three realms are separated and isolated from one another.
For what reason is this cessation further named "great salvation"?
Because it can ward off all great sufferings, calamities, and misfortunes.
For what reason is this cessation further called a refuge?
Because it is the basis for an intention and application that is free from falsehood.
Why is this cessation called the supreme refuge?
Because it serves as the basis for all most excellent noble natures that take refuge.
Why is this cessation further called the deathless?
Because it is forever free from birth.
Why is this cessation called "free from feverish affliction"?
Because it is forever free from the heat of all afflictions (*kleśa*), and because it is forever free from the great feverish affliction of the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.
For what reason is this cessation called "without burning"?
Because it is forever free from all sorrow, lamentation, grief, suffering, and various afflictions and disturbances.
For what reason is this cessation further called "peaceful"?
Because it is the basis for dwelling free from fear.
Why is this cessation further called "cool"?
Because it is the basis for all beneficial matters.
For what reason is this cessation further called a "blissful state"?
Because it is a blissful state in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
For what reason is this cessation called "leading to auspiciousness"?
It is for the sake of establishing the basis for the means of practice that are easy to cultivate.
Why is this cessation further named "freedom from disease"?
Because it is forever free from the diseases of all obstacles.
For what reason is this cessation also called "immovable"?
Because it is forever free from all agitation and movement.
For what reason is this cessation also called "nirvāṇa"?
Because it is the basis for the dwelling in the great bliss of signless quiescence.
Why is this cessation further called "non-arising"?
Because it is free from the continuity of rebirth.
For what reason is this cessation also called "non-arising"?
Because it is forever free from any subsequent gradual arising.
For what reason is this cessation also called "uncreated"?
Because it is forever free from being drawn forth by the power of past karma and afflictions.
Why is this cessation further called "non-action"?
Because it is not a basis for the performance of present karma and afflictions.
Why is this cessation also called "non-arising"?
Because it is forever free from the arising of future continuity.

Thus, the Truth of Cessation has four distinct characteristics: the characteristic of cessation, the characteristic of tranquility, the characteristic of excellence, and the characteristic of detachment.
What is the characteristic of cessation?
It is the dissociation from the afflictions (*kleśa*).
What is the characteristic of tranquility?
Because it is free from suffering.
What is its sublime characteristic?
Because it is the matter of delighting in tranquility.
What is meant by "being free from signs"?
It is because it constantly performs acts of benefit.
What is the Truth of the Path?

It means that by means of this path, one knows suffering, abandons the origin, realizes cessation, and cultivates the path; this is a brief description of the characteristics of the Truth of the Path.

There are five kinds of paths: the path of equipment (*sambhāra-mārga*), the path of application (*prayoga-mārga*), the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and the path of culmination (*niṣṭhā-mārga*).
What is the path of equipment (*sambhāramārga*)?

It refers to the ethical discipline (*śīla*) possessed by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, remaining constantly awake during the first and last watches of the night, and dwelling in right mindfulness while diligently cultivating tranquility (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).

Furthermore, there are other remaining wholesome qualities to be practiced: the wisdom arisen from hearing, the wisdom arisen from reflection, and the wisdom arisen from cultivation. By cultivating these, one attains the nature of being a vessel for the realization of clear observation and liberation.
What is the path of application (*prayogamārga*)?
It is said that all paths of equipment (*sambhāramārga*) are paths of application, though there are paths of application that are not paths of equipment.

These refer to the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*) belonging to one who has already accumulated the paths of equipment: namely, the stages of heat (*uṣmagata*), summits (*mūrdhan*), patience in accordance with the truths (*satyānulomikakṣānti*), and the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).
What is the stage of heat (*uṣmagata*)?
It refers to the concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and their associated factors, through which one individually and internally realizes the clear attainment regarding the [Four] Truths.
What is the stage of the summit (*mūrdhan*)?
It refers to the samādhi, prajñā, and their associated dharmas that increase clarity regarding the various truths through individual internal realization.
What are the dharmas of "patience in accordance with the truths" (satyānulomikī kṣānti)?
It refers to the wisdom (*prajñā*) and its associated factors that have individually and internally realized a portion of the truths and have entered into the conforming *samādhi*.
What is the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*)?
It refers to the uninterrupted mind-samādhi and prajñā regarding the truths, as well as the associated dharmas, which are individually and internally realized.
What is the path of seeing?
To state it in brief: it consists of the non-apprehending samādhi and prajñā that arise immediately after the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*), along with their associated factors;
furthermore, its characteristic is the wisdom of the absolute equality between the object of cognition and the cognizing subject.

Furthermore, it is characterized by the knowledge that universally eliminates both the provisional existence of individual sentient beings and the provisional existence of phenomena; it takes as its object the elimination of these two types of provisional existence. To explain the specific distinctions of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) individually:

they are the patience for the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñānakṣānti*), the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*), the subsequent patience for the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvayajñānakṣānti*), and the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvayajñāna*); the patience for the dharma-knowledge of origin (*samudaya-dharmajñānakṣānti*), the dharma-knowledge of origin (*samudaya-dharmajñāna*), the subsequent patience for the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvayajñānakṣānti*), and the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvayajñāna*); the patience for the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñānakṣānti*), the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñāna*), the subsequent patience for the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvayajñānakṣānti*), and the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvayajñāna*); and the patience for the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharmajñānakṣānti*), the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharmajñāna*), the subsequent patience for the knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvayajñānakṣānti*), and the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvayajñāna*). These follow immediately after the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).
These sixteen knowledges and patiences constitute the specific characteristics of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
What is suffering? It refers to the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
What is the dharma of suffering?
It refers to the teachings arising from the predominance of the Truth of Suffering.
What is the knowledge of dharmas (dharmajñāna)?
This refers to the knowledge (*jñāna*) that observes the dharmas predominant with the truths during the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*).
What is "receptivity to knowledge" (*jñāna-kṣānti*)?

It means that by the power of prior observation, one gives rise to uncontaminated wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) that realizes each individual truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). Because of this wisdom, one permanently abandons all afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering; therefore, it is called "receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*).
What is the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*)?

It refers to the realization of liberation from the aforementioned afflictions immediately following the stage of receptivity (*kṣānti*), by means of this knowledge; this is called the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering.
What is the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñānakṣānti*)?

It refers to the arising of uncontaminated wisdom immediately following the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna*), which internally realizes both the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering and that knowledge of the dharma itself, each individually.
It is said that all subsequent noble dharmas are of this same category; therefore, it is called the "receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñānakṣānti*).
What is the "subsequent knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñāna*)?

It refers to the arising of uncontaminated wisdom immediately following this [receptivity], which definitively ascertains and confirms the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering; this is called the subsequent knowledge of suffering.
In this manner, regarding the remaining truths, one should understand all the various patiences (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*) according to their respective applications.

Within this stage, one awakens to the apprehended (*grāhya*) through the dharma-patiences and dharma-knowledges, and awakens to the apprehender (*grāhaka*) through the subsequent patiences (*anvaya-kṣānti*) and subsequent knowledges (*anvaya-jñāna*).
Furthermore, within this entire stage of patience and knowledge, one is said to be "abiding in the contemplation of the signless.
These sixteen moments of mind are called the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga).
The ultimate arising of cognition regarding the objects of knowledge is termed a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).
All truths of the path (*mārgasatya*) are to be realized through four modes of application: namely, by way of establishment, by way of reflection, by way of realization, and by way of fulfillment.
What is meant by "establishment"?

It refers to śrāvakas and others who, having attained the ultimate according to their own realization, desire to cause others to understand it as well; thus, by means of subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), they establish the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) through immeasurable sets of names, phrases, and syllables (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*).
What is meant by "by way of reflection"?
It refers to the correct cultivation of the means for clear realization (*abhisamaya*), reflecting upon and repeatedly practicing with mundane knowledge according to how things are established.
What is meant by "by way of realization and experience"?
This refers to having thus repeatedly practiced, one personally realizes within oneself the initial stage of the path of seeing, which is supramundane and free from conceptual proliferation.
How is this perfected? It means that following this stage, there is the perfection of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), culminating in the attainment of the ultimate.

Once he has realized the ultimate stage, he further establishes the Truth of the Path by means of the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) through the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*).

As stated in the Sūtra: "Having removed the dust and abandoned the defilement, the pure Dharma-eye arises regarding all phenomena. This is said with reference to the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*); the various *dharmakṣāntis* (patiences) remove the dust, while the various *dharmanatis* (knowledges) abandon the defilement.
Because of thorough knowledge and because of permanent abandonment, the path attains purity.
As stated in the Sūtra:

"One sees the Dharma, attains the Dharma, thoroughly penetrates the Dharma, and reaches the ultimate firmness of the Dharma; one transcends all longing and doubt, and does not rely on others as conditions."
Regarding the teaching of the Great Master, one cannot be led astray by others and attains fearlessness concerning all phenomena;
this is also explained in reference to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
"Seeing the phenomena" refers to the various patiences (*kṣānti*) regarding the phenomena.
"Attaining the Dharma" refers to the various knowledges (*jñāna*) regarding phenomena.
"Thoroughly penetrating the Dharma" refers to the various types of receptivities (*kṣānti*).
"Ultimately firm in the Dharma" refers to the various types of knowledges (*jñāna*).
"Transcending all expectations" means that, by virtue of various patiences and knowledges, one has no expectation or anxiety regarding what one has realized for oneself.
"Transcending all doubts" means that, within this stage, one has no hesitation regarding what others have realized.
"Not depending on other conditions" means that within the path being cultivated, there is no guidance by others, but rather natural skillfulness.
Regarding "that which cannot be led astray from the Great Teacher’s instruction by others," this means that within the Buddha’s holy teaching, one is not diverted or led away by false paths.
Regarding "attaining fearlessness among all phenomena": this is because, within the context of answering questions concerning the realized dharma, any timid or inferior mind is forever absent.
What is the path of cultivation?

That is to say, all paths belonging to the path of vision—namely, the mundane path, the supramundane path, the weak path, the middling path, the superior path, the path of preparation, the uninterrupted path, the path of liberation, the path of advancement, and so forth—are called the path of cultivation.
What is the mundane path?

It refers to the mundane first dhyāna, second dhyāna, third dhyāna, and fourth dhyāna; and the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

In this way, the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and formless attainments (*ārūpya*) should be analyzed extensively by way of four aspects: namely, in terms of affliction (*saṃkleśa*), purity (*śukla*), establishment (*vyavasthāna*), and purification (*viśuddhi*).
What constitutes defilement?
It refers to the four indeterminate roots:
first, craving; second, views; third, pride; and fourth, ignorance.

Due to craving (*tṛṣṇā*), one is defiled by the defilement of attachment to the higher dhyānas; due to views (*dṛṣṭi*), one is defiled by the defilement of attachment to the higher dhyānas through views; due to pride (*māna*), one is defiled by the defilement of attachment to the higher dhyānas through pride; and due to ignorance (*avidyā*), one is defiled by the defilement of attachment to the higher dhyānas through doubt (*vicikitsā*).
In this way, these afflictions constantly defile the mind, causing the afflictions and secondary afflictions of the form and formless realms to flow on in succession.
Why is it called "pure and white"?
This refers to the pure dhyānas and formless attainments, which are termed "pure and white" because they are virtuous by nature.

By what means are they established? There are four types of establishment: namely, establishment by way of factors (*aṅga*), establishment by way of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), establishment by way of categories (*prakāra*), and establishment by way of designations (*saṃjñā*).
How are the factors established?
It is said that the first dhyāna has five factors. What are these five?
First, applied thought; second, sustained thought; third, joy; fourth, bliss; fifth, one-pointedness of mind.
The second dhyāna has four factors. What are these four?
First, internal serenity; second, joy; third, bliss; fourth, one-pointedness of mind.
The third dhyāna has five factors. What are these five?
First, equanimity; second, mindfulness; third, clear comprehension; fourth, bliss; fifth, one-pointedness of mind.
The fourth dhyāna has four factors. What are these four?
First, purity through equanimity;
second, purity through mindfulness;
third, the sensation of neither-pain-nor-pleasure?

The one-pointedness of mind is not established as a constituent among the formless attainments because it is of a single flavor with *śamatha*. This is because [the other constituents] serve as the antidotal factors, the beneficial factors, and the essential nature factor upon which those two depend.
What is the establishment of the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*)?

It refers to entering the first *dhyāna* by means of seven types of mental attention (*manasikāra*), and so on, up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
What are the seven types of mental engagement (*manasikāra*)?

They are: mental engagement that discerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇapratisaṃvedī*), mental engagement of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣika*), mental engagement of detachment (*prāvivekya*), mental engagement of delight in withdrawal (*ratisaṃgrāhaka*), mental engagement of investigation (*mīmāṃsā*), mental engagement of the culmination of application (*prayoganiṣṭha*), and mental engagement of the fruit of the culmination of application (*prayoganiṣṭhāphala*).
What is the establishment by way of categories?
It refers to the cultivation of the first dhyāna in three grades—mild, medium, and superior.
As it is with the first dhyāna, so it is for the remaining dhyānas and the formless attainments regarding their cultivation in these three grades.
Due to the cultivation of the first dhyāna through weak, medium, and superior degrees, three types of karmic maturation arise within that first dhyāna.
Just as it is with the first dhyāna, so it is for the other dhyānas: both their cultivation and the resulting fruits each consist of three grades.
Because there are no distinct locations within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), no differentiation of birthplaces for the arising of results is established.

Nevertheless, due to the cultivation of the formless absorptions (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) in three grades, when their maturation (*vipāka*) arises, there are distinctions of high and low, and of inferior and superior.
What is meant by "establishing names and concepts"?

It refers to the samādhis entered by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have attained ultimate great majesty within the meditative concentrations included in the first dhyāna. Even all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not understand the names of those samādhis, much less could they know their number.
How much more so for actual realization?
As it is with the meditative concentrations included within the first dhyāna, so it is with those included within the other dhyānas and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
All that has been explained thus far relies upon the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).
What is purity?
It refers to the ultimate concentration within the first dhyāna, up to and including the ultimate concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is called purity.
What is the supramundane path?

It refers to the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path—comprised within the categories of dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) during the path of cultivation—as well as the associated samādhis and so forth. These are either comprised within the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) or comprised within the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). As for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), it is exclusively mundane because an unclear perception (*asaṃprakhyāna-saṃjñā*) constantly operates therein; for this reason, it is called "non-perception" (*asaṃjñā*).
As the Blessed One said:
"Up to the attainment of the meditative absorption with perception (*saṃjñā-samāpatti*), one is able to illuminate and penetrate reality as it truly is.
The attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is likewise included within the supramundane (*lokottara*), because it is realized subsequent to the Noble Path (*ārya-mārga*).

It can only be induced within the human realm; it may manifest either in the human realm or in the form realm, but it generally does not arise when one is born in the formless realm. This is because those who abide in the maturation of the liberation of tranquility do not frequently initiate this meditative attainment of cessation, as they lack the application of diligent effort.
What is the weak path?
It refers to the weak-weak, weak-middle, and weak-superior paths.

By means of these paths, one is able to abandon the three grades of afflictions—namely, the superior-superior, superior-middle, and superior-inferior—within each stage (bhūmi) bound to the three realms.
What is the middle path?
It refers to the middling-soft, the middling-middling, and the middling-superior grades of the path.
By means of this path, one is able to abandon the three grades of afflictions—middling-superior, middling-middling, and middling-soft—belonging to each stage within the triple world.
What is the superior path?
It refers to the superior-soft, superior-middle, and superior-superior grades of the path.
By means of this path, one is able to abandon the three grades of afflictions—namely, the superior-soft, superior-middle, and superior-soft-soft—pertaining to each stage within the three realms.
What is the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*)?
It refers to that path by which one is able to abandon the afflictions; this is called the path of preparation within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
What is the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*)?
This refers to the path by which, immediately thereafter, one eternally severs the afflictions so that nothing remains.
What is the path of liberation?
It refers to the path by which one realizes the liberation obtained through the severance of those afflictions.
What is the path of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*)?

It refers to all paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*), and paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) for the purpose of abandoning the remaining categories of afflictions; these are called the path of superior progress.

Furthermore, whether one abandons the application for abandoning afflictions and diligently contemplates various phenomena, or diligently abides in various phenomena, or progresses to cultivate other meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), all such paths are called the path of superior progress.
Furthermore, that which brings forth superior qualities or causes one to abide in all the various paths is called the path of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*).
How, then, should these paths be cultivated?

These are: cultivation by acquisition (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*), cultivation by practice (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*), cultivation by removal (*vinirdhāvana-bhāvanā*), and cultivation by antidote (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*).
Cultivation by acquisition refers to the cultivation of wholesome dharmas not yet arisen, so that they may arise.
Cultivation by practice refers to the cultivation of wholesome dharmas already arisen, so that they may remain firm, be not forgotten, and increase further and further.
The cultivation of removal refers to cultivating the already arisen unwholesome and unvirtuous states so that they are permanently severed.
The cultivation of the antidote refers to cultivating the as-yet-unarisen unwholesome and unvirtuous states so that they do not arise.
Furthermore, when the path arises, it is able to establish its own habitual tendencies; this is called "cultivation through attainment" (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*).
When this very path is cultivated as it manifests before one, this is called "cultivation through practice" (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*).
When this very path is present before one, it is able to abandon its own obstacles; this is called "cultivation through removal" (*vinirdhāvana-bhāvanā*).
When this very path abandons its own obstacles and causes those [obstacles] in the future to abide in the state of non-arising, it is called the cultivation of the antidote (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*).

Furthermore, there are four kinds of antidotes that are termed the cultivation of the antidote: namely, the antidote of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇa-pratipakṣa*), the antidote of abandonment (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*), the antidote of maintenance (*dhāraṇa-pratipakṣa*), and the antidote of distancing (*dūrībhāva-pratipakṣa*).
What is the antidote of revulsion?
It refers to seeing many faults and afflictions in all contaminated conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
What is the antidote of abandonment?
This refers to the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) and the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*).
What is the antidote of maintenance (*dhāraṇa-pratipakṣa*)?
It refers to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
What is the antidote by way of distance?
It refers to all subsequent paths.

Furthermore, there are eleven distinctions of the path: the path of investigating phenomena, the path of diligent application, the path of cultivating meditative concentration, the path of the means to clear realization, the path of approaching clear realization, the path of clear realization, the path of pure renunciation, the path according to the distinctions of faculties, the path of purifying the three trainings, the path of generating all virtues, and the path that universally encompasses all paths.

These paths follow their respective order: namely, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the four kinds of right practice, the four bases of spiritual power, serenity (*śamatha*), insight (*vipaśyanā*), and the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).

In this context, all factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) are established by way of five doors: namely, by way of their object (ālambana), their essential nature (svabhāva), their companions (sahāya), their cultivation (bhāvanā), and the fruit of cultivation (bhāvanāphala).
Regarding the objects of the four foundations of mindfulness, they are body, sensation, mind, and phenomena.
Furthermore, there are four matters: the matter of what I rely upon, the matter of what I enjoy, the matter of my own self-essence, and the matter of my defilement and purification.
The essential nature consists of wisdom and mindfulness.
The accompanying factors consist of the mind and mental concomitants associated with them.
Cultivation refers to practicing the contemplation of the body and so forth with respect to the internal body and so forth.
As it is with the internal, so it is with the external and with both the internal and external.
"Internal body" refers to all internal bases of form within this body.
"External body" refers to all external bases of form outside of this body.

Regarding the internal-external body: it refers to all external bases (*bāhyāyatana*) associated with the internal bases that serve as the support for the sense faculties (*indriya*), as well as all internal form-bases (*rūpāyatana*) within the bodies of others.
How does one practice the contemplation of the body in the body?
This means that one contemplates internal feeling by regarding it as equal to the body of the conceptual image and the essential body.
Internal feeling refers to feeling produced based on the internal body;
external feeling refers to feeling produced based on the external body.
Internal and external feeling refers to the feelings produced based on the internal and external body.
As it is with feeling, so it is with the mind and mental phenomena.
Just as one cultivates the contemplation of the body in relation to the body, so too one cultivates the contemplation of feelings and so forth in relation to feelings and so forth, as appropriate.

Furthermore, as for cultivation, it refers to desire, diligence, exertion, perseverance, heroism, non-cessation, right mindfulness, right awareness, and heedfulness, due to the distinctions in cultivation.
"Cultivating" refers to the practice undertaken as an antidote to the secondary affliction of non-attention (*amanasikāra*).
"Diligently cultivating" refers to the practice undertaken as an antidote to the secondary affliction of laziness (*kausīdya*).
"Exerting cultivation" refers to the practice undertaken as an antidote to the secondary afflictions of lethargy and restlessness.
"Vigorous cultivation" refers to the practice undertaken as an antidote to the secondary affliction of mental inferiority.
"Vigorously practicing" refers to the application of practice as an antidote to the secondary afflictions of negligence and fatigue.

"Practicing without ceasing" refers to the application of practice as an antidote to the secondary affliction of becoming complacent and satisfied with having attained only a small amount of wholesome dharmas.
The cultivation of right mindfulness refers to the counteracting of the secondary affliction of forgetting the sublime teachings.
The cultivation of right awareness refers to the counteracting of the secondary affliction of remorse for transgressions.
The cultivation of heedfulness refers to the counteracting of the secondary affliction that abandons all wholesome yokes.
Its fruit consists of the severance of the four perversions, the entry into the Four Noble Truths, and the dissociation of the body and so forth from bondage.
Regarding the objects of the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*): they are the factors to be abandoned and their antidotes, whether already arisen or yet to arise.
Their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is diligence (*vīrya*).
Their attendants (*sahāya*) are the mind and mental factors associated with them.
Regarding cultivation, as stated in the sūtras:
"One generates desire, exerts oneself, arouses right effort, and sustains and upholds the mind.
Herein, these phrases clarify the cultivation of right effort and its basis.
The basis is desire (*chanda*).
Right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*) refers to exertion and so forth.

Within the mental attentions (*manasikāra*) regarding the signs of tranquility (*śamatha*), arousal (*pragraha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), one exerts right effort in order to diminish lethargy (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya); therefore, it is said next that one "exerts the mind" and "sustains the mind."
The fruit of cultivation refers to the complete relinquishing of all that is to be abandoned (*pratipakṣya*).
Whether it be the attainment or the increase of the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*), this is called the fruit of cultivation.
The object of focus (*ālambana*) for the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) refers to the tasks to be accomplished once meditative concentration has been perfected.
The essential nature refers to samādhi.
The accompanying factors refer to desire, effort, mind, and investigation, as well as the primary minds and mental factors associated with them.
What is the concentration of desire?
It is the attainment of one-pointedness of mind through earnest application.
What is the concentration of exertion?
That is to say, by means of uninterrupted application, one touches upon one-pointedness of mind.
What is concentration of mind?
It is that which, through the power of previously cultivated concentration, touches upon one-pointedness of mind.
What is the concentration of observation?
It refers to the attainment of one-pointedness of mind through internal discernment based on hearing the teachings of others.
Furthermore, the concentration of desire refers to the attainment of one-pointedness of mind by generating desire.
Vigor concentration (*vīrya-samādhi*) refers to the contact with one-pointedness of mind through the exertion of right effort.
Mind concentration (*citta-samādhi*) refers to the contact with one-pointedness of mind through the stabilization of the mind.
Regarding the samādhi of observation: it refers to touching one-pointedness of mind by means of exerting the mind.
Regarding its cultivation: it refers to repeatedly practicing the eight types of formative actions of abandonment. What are these eight?
These are: desire, diligence, faith, tranquility, right mindfulness, right situational awareness, volition, and equanimity.
These eight types are briefly subsumed into four categories: application, acquisition, continuity, and antidote.

Furthermore, there are two types of cultivation through desire, diligence, mind, and investigation: namely, cultivation that involves the gathering and dispersing of causes and conditions along with their distancing, and cultivation that accords with and relies upon those two [states] of being neither inferior nor distracted.

Regarding the fruit of cultivation: because one has already thoroughly refined and cultivated samādhi, one is able to penetrate and manifest, in accordance with the mind, whatever dharmas one wishes to realize or penetrate.

Furthermore, within various distinct phenomena, one realizes the capacity for mastery and functional efficacy; thus, according to one's aspirations and inclinations, one can accomplish various feats such as supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) and can further induce superior qualities (*guṇa*).
The objects of the five faculties are the four noble truths.
Their essential natures are faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
Their attendants are the associated mind and mental factors.
Regarding cultivation: it means that through the faculty of faith, one cultivates the practice of patience and acceptance toward the truths;
and through the faculty of diligence, once patience and acceptance toward the truths have arisen, one cultivates the practice of diligent application for the sake of awakening.
Having exerted diligence regarding the various truths through the faculty of mindfulness, one cultivates the practice of establishing mindfulness so that it does not become lost.
Having established mindfulness regarding the various truths through the faculty of concentration, one cultivates the practice of one-pointedness of mind.
Regarding the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), once the mind has attained concentration with respect to the truths, one engages in the practice of discernment (*pravicaya*).

As for the fruit of this cultivation, it means being able to swiftly give rise to the direct realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*), as well as being able to cultivate and refine the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and Summits (*mūrdhan*), thereby inducing Patience (*kṣānti*) and the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).
As it is with the five faculties, so it is with the five powers (*pañca-balāni*).
The distinction is that because these can diminish the opposing obstacles and cannot be overcome, they are called "powers."
The object of the seven factors of enlightenment is the suchness of the four noble truths.
Their essential nature consists of mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.
Mindfulness is the factor of support;
the investigation of dharmas is the factor of essential nature;
and diligence is the factor of emergence.
Joy is the factor of benefit.

Tranquility, concentration, and equanimity are the factors of non-defilement; this is because they are non-defiled by nature, because they rely upon what is non-defiled, and because their essential substance is non-defiled.
The "concomitants" refer to the associated mind and mental factors.
"Cultivation" refers to cultivating the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness by relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, and relying on cessation, and by dedicating it toward relinquishment.
As it is with the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, so it is for each up to the factor of enlightenment of equanimity.
These four propositions sequentially demonstrate the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment by taking the objects of the Four Noble Truths as their domain.
The fruit of cultivation refers to the permanent abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing.
The object of focus for the eight branches of the noble path refers to the suchness of these very same Four Noble Truths at a subsequent time.
As for its essential nature, it consists of right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
Right view is the factor of discernment;
right intention is the factor of instructing others;
and right speech, right action, and right livelihood are the factors for inspiring confidence in others, because they constitute the purity of view, conduct, and livelihood.
Right effort is the limb that purifies the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Right mindfulness is the limb that purifies the obstacle of secondary afflictions (*upakleśāvaraṇa*).
Right concentration is the limb that can purify the obstacle to supreme qualities (*guṇaviśeṣāvaraṇa*).
The companions are the associated mind and mental factors.
As for cultivation, it is as explained in the section on the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).

As for the fruit of cultivation, it refers to providing analytical instruction to others so that they may gain faith, thereby purifying the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), the hindrances of secondary afflictions (*upakleśāvaraṇa*), and the hindrances to supreme qualities (*viśeṣaguṇāvaraṇa*).

There are four types of practitioners of the right path: those with difficult progress and slow comprehension, those with difficult progress and quick comprehension, those with easy progress and slow comprehension, and those with easy progress and quick comprehension.

The first refers to those of dull faculties who have not yet attained the fundamental dhyānas; the second refers to those of sharp faculties who have not yet attained the fundamental dhyānas; the third refers to those of dull faculties who have already attained the fundamental dhyānas; and the fourth refers to those of sharp faculties who have already attained the fundamental dhyānas.
The four tracks of the Dharma are non-attachment, non-hatred, right mindfulness, and right concentration.

Non-attachment and non-hatred enable the purification of the training in higher ethics; right mindfulness enables the purification of the training in higher mind; and right concentration enables the purification of the training in higher wisdom.

Śamatha refers to withdrawing the mind within so that it abides, abides evenly, abides securely, and abides closely; it is the taming, the pacifying, and the supreme pacification of the mind, focusing it on a single object and maintaining it in equanimity.

Vipaśyanā refers to the discernment of phenomena, supreme discernment, universal investigation, and thorough examination; it is for the purpose of counteracting the fetters of coarse and heavy characteristics, for the purpose of subduing all perversions, and to cause the non-perverted mind to abide well.
Furthermore, four types of paths are established based on śamatha and vipaśyanā.
There may be a certain class of individuals who have already attained śamatha but not vipaśyanā; such individuals advance toward the cultivation of vipaśyanā by relying upon śamatha.
There may be a certain class of persons who have attained vipaśyanā but not śamatha; such individuals rely on vipaśyanā to further cultivate śamatha.

There may be another class who have attained neither śamatha nor vipaśyanā; such individuals apply their minds with single-minded focus to subdue lethargy and agitation, cultivating both paths simultaneously.

There may be a certain class of persons who have already attained both śamatha and vipaśyanā; for such individuals, these two paths of śamatha and vipaśyanā operate in unison, in equilibrium, and as a unified pair.

The three faculties are the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*), and the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
What is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"?
It refers to all the faculties present during the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) and during the fifteen moments of mind within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
What is the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātendriya*)?
It refers to all faculties present within the path of those in training (*śaikṣa*) from the sixteenth moment of mind of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) onwards.
What is the faculty of one who has perfect knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*)? It refers to all the faculties belonging to the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).

When one practices the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) based on the stage of the first dhyāna, one also cultivates all the wholesome roots associated with the desire realm, because one has attained mastery over them.

Just as one cultivates the wholesome roots of the desire realm by relying on the stage of the first dhyāna, so too, when practicing the path of cultivation while relying on any of the higher stages, one is able to cultivate all the wholesome roots belonging to the lower realms and lower stages, because one has attained mastery over them.
What is the ultimate path?

It refers to that which, by relying on the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), results in the eternal cessation of all coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*), the eternal severance of all acquisitions of bondage (*bandhana-prāpti*), and the eternal realization of all acquisitions of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-prāpti*). Following this, there occurs a successive and uninterrupted transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), whereby one realizes the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), and the ten qualities of those beyond training (*aśaikṣadharma*).
What are these ten?

They are the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), up to the right concentration of one beyond training; the right liberation of one beyond training; and the right knowledge of one beyond training.
Such dharmas as these are called the ultimate path (*niṣṭhāmārga*).
What are called all the *dausthulyas* (burdensome dysfunctions)? Briefly stated, there are twenty-four kinds: namely, the pervasive conceptual proliferation *dausthulya*;

the *dausthulya* of experience; the *dausthulya* of afflictions; the *dausthulya* of karma; the *dausthulya* of maturation; the *dausthulya* of the affliction-obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*); the *dausthulya* of the karma-obstruction (*karmāvaraṇa*); the *dausthulya* of the maturation-obstruction (*vipākāvaraṇa*); the *dausthulya* of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*); the *dausthulya* of discursive thought (*vitarka*); the *dausthulya* of food and drink; the *dausthulya* of sexual union; the *dausthulya* of dreams; the *dausthulya* of illness; the *dausthulya* of aging; the *dausthulya* of death; the *dausthulya* of fatigue; the solid *dausthulya*; the coarse *dausthulya*; the middling *dausthulya*; the subtle *dausthulya*; the *dausthulya* of the affliction-obstruction; the *dausthulya* of the meditative concentration-obstruction (*samādhāvaraṇa*); and the *dausthulya* of the cognitive-obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
What is the acquisition of bondage (*bandhana-prāpti*)?
It refers to the nature of the acquisition of bondage, which is a conventional designation for the accumulation of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*).
What is the acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*)?
This refers to the nature of the attainment of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*), which is conventionally designated upon the dispersal of the heavy residues (*dausthulya*).
What is the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*)?

It refers to the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) existing at the stage of the final path of abandonment within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), which is comprised either of the preparatory path (*prayogamārga*) or the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*).
That which is subsumed under the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) refers to that from which point onward one is no longer obstructed by any hindrances and is able to destroy all hindrances.

That which is subsumed under the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) refers to that from which the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) arise immediately thereafter.
Furthermore, this samādhi is uninterrupted, firm, of a single flavor, and all-pervading; to illustrate this meaning, the Bhagavān said:
"It is like a great mountain of stone—without fissures, without gaps, without holes, a single solid mass, perfectly complete—which cannot be moved or shaken by fierce winds from the ten directions."
What is called the uninterrupted transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parivṛtti*)?
It refers to the threefold transformation of the basis attained by one who has already realized the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*).
What are these three?
This refers to the transformation of the basis of the mind, the transformation of the basis of the path, and the transformation of the basis of the heavy impediments.
What is the knowledge of exhaustion?
It is the knowledge obtained through the exhaustion of causes, or that which takes exhaustion as its object.
What is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*)?
It refers to the knowledge obtained through the abandonment of the fruit,
or that which takes the non-arising of the fruit as its object.

The ten qualities of one beyond training (aśaikṣadharma) should be understood as being taught in reliance upon the aggregate of morality, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation of one beyond training.

Thus, the truth of the path (mārgasatya) generally has four distinct aspects of practice: namely, the aspect of the path (*mārgākāra*), the aspect of correctness (*nyāyākāra*), the aspect of practice (*pratipadākāra*), and the aspect of deliverance (*nairyāṇikākāra*).
What is the aspect of the path?
Therefore, because one seeks the true meaning,
what is its characteristic?
It is that which can serve as the antidote to all afflictions.
What is the aspect of practice?
It is the ability to effectively accomplish the mind so that it does not become inverted.
What is the aspect of emergence?
Because they lead toward the track of true permanence,
all sixteen aspects (*ākāra*) among the various truths (*satya*) pertain to both the mundane (*laukika*) and the supramundane (*lokottara*).
What is the distinction between the mundane and the supramundane?

Because there is a distinction between the nature of not correctly entering and correctly entering the objects of knowledge; because there is a distinction between the nature of being obstructed and being unobstructed; and because there is a distinction between the nature of being conceptual and being non-conceptual.

Why is this so? Because within the various truths, one has not skillfully realized the sixteen worldly modes of perception—such as impermanence, suffering, and so forth—with respect to the nature of *tathatā* (suchness); because afflictions remain latent (*anuśaya*) therein; and because one gives rise to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) by relying on the gateway of conventional designations.
The mode of supramundane practice is the opposite of this.

When the mode of supramundane practice manifests, although one directly realizes and perceives the meaning of impermanence, one does not perceive "this is the meaning of impermanence" by way of the gateway of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) involving names and expressions.
Just as the aspect of impermanence relates to the object of impermanence, it should be understood that other aspects relate to their respective objects in the same manner, as appropriate.
