Section Two: The Determination of Phenomena (Dharmaviniścaya). Within the Determination of Phenomena, Chapter Two: Phenomena. What is the determination of phenomena?
"Dharma" refers to the twelvefold collection of the noble teachings (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*).

What are these twelve? First, the discourses (*sūtra*); second, the verses (*geya*); third, the prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*); fourth, the stanzas (*gāthā*); fifth, the spontaneous utterances (*udāna*); sixth, the causal origins (*nidāna*); seventh, the parables (*avadāna*); eighth, the past events (*itivṛttaka*); ninth, the birth stories (*jātaka*); tenth, the extensive teachings (*vaipulya*); eleventh, the marvelous qualities (*adbhutadharma*); and twelfth, the analytical treatises (*upadeśa*).
What is a *sūtra*? It refers to a concise exposition of the meanings that ought to be explained, composed in prose.

Having observed ten kinds of benefits, the Tathāgata compiled these prose compositions to briefly explain all phenomena (*dharma*). These are: it is easy to establish; it is easy to proclaim; it is easy to receive and uphold; because of reverence for the Dharma, the provisions for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*) are swiftly brought to fulfillment; one is able to quickly penetrate the true nature of all phenomena; one attains verified pure faith (*avetyaprasāda*) toward the Buddhas; one attains verified pure faith toward the Dharma and the Saṅgha; one realizes the supreme dwelling in happiness in this very life (*dr̥ṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*); it delights the minds of the wise through discussion and definitive resolution; and one gains entry into the ranks of the intelligent and the sagacious.
What is the *geya* (verses to be recited)?
It refers to those sūtras that are either interspersed with or followed by verses (*gāthā*) as a re-recitation.
Furthermore, because sūtras of incomplete meaning (*neyārtha*) require further explanation through verse, they are called *geya*.
What is *vyākaraṇa* (prophecy)?
It refers to the prophecy concerning the gains, losses, and distinctions of birth-places for noble disciples (*āryaśrāvaka*) who have passed away into the past.
Furthermore, definitive sūtras (*nītārtha-sūtra*) clarify *vyākaraṇa*, because it reveals the profound and hidden intention (*saṃdhi*).
What is *geya* (verses)?
It refers to those discourses taught in the sūtras by means of verses, consisting of two lines, or three, four, five, or six.
What is *udāna* (inspired utterances)?
This refers to those sūtras in which the Tathāgata, being pleased in mind, speaks of his own accord.
What is the *nidāna* (circumstantial origin)?
It refers to that which is spoken in response to a request.
Furthermore, there are also cases where training rules (śikṣāpada) are established based on specific causes and conditions; these are likewise called "origins" (nidāna).
What are similes? They refer to those discourses (sūtra) that contain explanations by way of analogies.
What is it that constitutes *itivṛttaka*?
It refers to the proclamation of events concerning the previous lives of the noble disciples and others.
What is it that constitutes *jātaka*?
It refers to the teaching of matters corresponding to the *Pūrvayoga-vaipulya* (the Storehouse of the Bodhisattva’s Past Deeds).
What is the *Vaipulya*?
It refers to the discourse corresponding to the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka*.
That which is called Vaipulya is also called Vaitulya and Anuttara.
For what reason is it called Vaipulya?
Because it is the locus upon which all sentient beings rely for their benefit and happiness, and because it proclaims the vast and profound Dharma.
For what reason is it called "Extensive Destruction"?
Because it is able extensively to destroy all obstacles.
For what reason is it called "Peerless"?
Because there are no phenomena that can serve as a comparison for it.
What is this marvelous phenomenon?
It refers to those instances where the most extremely rare, most extraordinary, and most wondrous dharmas of the śrāvakas, the great bodhisattvas, and the Tathāgatas are proclaimed.
What is the exposition (upadeśa)?
It is that wherein all profound and hidden characteristics of phenomena are explained without error.
Such twelvefold divisions of the sūtras and so forth are subsumed within the Three Piṭakas of the Noble Teaching.
What are the three?
First, the Sūtra Piṭaka; second, the Vinaya Piṭaka; third, the Abhidharma Piṭaka.
These, in turn, are of two kinds:
First, the Śrāvaka-piṭaka; second, the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
These five—sūtra, geya, vyākaraṇa, gāthā, and udāna—are subsumed within the Sūtra-piṭaka of the Śrāvaka-piṭaka.

These four—dependent origination (nidāna), parables (avadāna), past events (itivṛttaka), and birth stories (jātaka)—are subsumed within the Vinaya Piṭaka along with its ancillaries among the two Piṭakas.
The two categories of extensive teachings (vaipulya) and marvelous qualities (adbhutadharma) are subsumed within the Sūtra Piṭaka of the Bodhisattva Piṭaka.
The category of discourses on debate (*upadeśa*) is subsumed within the Abhidharma Piṭaka among the two collections of the Śrāvaka and Bodhisattva vehicles.
For what reason did the Tathāgata establish the three collections?
He established the Sūtra Piṭaka for the purpose of counteracting the secondary affliction of doubt.
The Vinaya Piṭaka is established to counteract the secondary afflictions associated with the two extremes of enjoyment;
the Abhidharma Piṭaka is established to counteract the secondary affliction of attachment to one's own views.
Furthermore, the Sūtra Piṭaka is established in order to reveal the three types of training;
the Vinaya Piṭaka is established in order to establish the training in higher ethics and the training in higher mind;
and the Abhidharma Piṭaka is established in order to establish the training in higher wisdom.
Furthermore, the Sūtra Piṭaka is established in order to reveal the meaning of the True Dharma;
the Vinaya Piṭaka is established to manifest the basis for the realization and establishment of the meaning of the Dharma;
and the Abhidharma Piṭaka is established so that the wise may engage in debate and discernment, thereby enjoying the dwelling in the bliss of the Dharma.
For whom are these phenomena included within the Three Pitakas the domain?
They are the domain of the mental states and mental factors consisting of what is produced by hearing, what is produced by reflection, and what is produced by cultivation.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"All mental states and mental factors have an object of cognition (ālambana), a mode of apprehension (ākāra), a basis (āśraya), and are associated (samprayukta).
With respect to these phenomena, what is their object of cognition?
This refers to the sūtras and so forth.
What is their mode of operation?
It is the meaning associated with the aggregates and so forth.
What is its basis?
It is the manifest expression of others, recollection, and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
What is its association?
This means that they act as mutual companions, achieving a uniform understanding of the object and its aspects.
What are the distinctions among the objects of the dharmas?
Briefly stated, there are four types: the pervasive object, the object for purifying conduct, the object for skillfulness, and the object for purifying afflictions.

The pervasive objects of focus are further of four kinds: namely, the object of focus that is a conceptual image, the object of focus that is a non-conceptual image, the object of focus that is the limit of phenomena, and the object of focus that is the accomplishment of what was to be done.

The object of focus consisting of an image with conceptual differentiation refers to the objective domain of all śamatha and vipaśyanā resulting from mental attention through resolute conviction (adhimokṣa-manasikāra).
The object of focus consisting of non-conceptual images refers to the objective domain of all śamatha and vipaśyanā resulting from correct mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*).
The object of focus regarding the limits of phenomena refers to the "extent of existence" (yāvadbhāvikatā) and the "mode of existence" (yathāvadbhāvikatā) of all dharmas.
The extent of existence refers to the aggregates, elements, and sense bases.

The nature of things as they are refers to the sixteen aspects of the four noble truths, suchness, the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena, the suffering of all conditioned phenomena, the selflessness of all phenomena, the tranquility of nirvana, and emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness.
Regarding the object of focus for the accomplishment of what is to be done, this refers to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*); such a transformation of the basis is inconceivable.
Among the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*), how many aspects are subsumed under emptiness (*śūnyatā*)?
It refers to two.
How many aspects (ākāra) are subsumed under the wishless (apraṇihita)?
It refers to six.
How many aspects (*ākāra*) are subsumed under the signless (*animitta*)? There are eight.

Furthermore, there are five objects of focus for pure conduct (*śubha-viṣaya*): namely, one who is dominated by greed focuses on the object of impurity (*aśubhā*); one dominated by hatred focuses on the object of cultivating loving-kindness (*maitrī*); one dominated by delusion focuses on the object of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) consisting of various conditions; one dominated by pride focuses on the object of the differentiation of elements (*dhātu-prabheda*); and one dominated by discursive thought focuses on the object of mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation (*ānāpānasmṛti*).

Skillfulness regarding the objects of focus also consists of five types, namely: skillfulness regarding the aggregates, skillfulness regarding the elements, skillfulness regarding the sense bases, skillfulness regarding dependent origination, and skillfulness regarding what is possible and what is impossible.
How should one contemplate skillfulness regarding what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-kauśalya*)?
One should contemplate it as one contemplates skillfulness regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*).
What is the difference between skillfulness regarding what is possible and impossible and skillfulness regarding dependent origination?

If one uses all phenomena to moisten all phenomena, causing them to be free from arising without cause or from unequal causes, this is skillfulness regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Because it involves the harmonious correspondence of cause and effect and the gathering together of birth, this is skillfulness regarding what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-kauśalya*).

The objects of focus for purifying afflictions refer to the coarseness of the lower stages, the tranquility of the higher stages, suchness, and the four noble truths; these are called the objects of focus for purifying afflictions.
If one wishes to diligently and carefully examine phenomena, by how many principles can one correctly examine them?

By four principles: namely, the principle of dependence (*apekṣā-yukti*), the principle of efficacy (*kāryakāraṇa-yukti*), the principle of logical proof (*upapatti-sādhana-yukti*), and the principle of natural law (*dharmatā-yukti*).
What is the principle of dependence?
It means that when conditioned phenomena arise, they necessarily depend upon a collection of conditions.
What is the principle of functional efficacy?
This refers to the distinct functions of various phenomena characterized by different marks.
What is the principle of logical proof?
It is the proclamation of statements that do not contradict the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in order to establish a meaning that is yet to be proven.
What is the principle of the nature of things (*dharmatā-yukti*)?

It refers to the established nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), which exists as the very nature of things within all phenomena—whether characterized by their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) or general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)—from beginningless time.
Regarding the correct and diligent observation of all phenomena, how does one engage in the investigation of phenomena?
It refers to the arising of four kinds of investigation:

first, the investigation of names; second, the investigation of things; third, the investigation of the designation of intrinsic nature; and fourth, the investigation of the designation of distinctions.
What is the investigation of names?
It refers to the analytical search for the self-characteristics of the collections of names, phrases, and phonemes of all phenomena, finding that none of them are established as real.
What is the investigation of things?
This refers to investigating how the characteristics of all phenomena—the aggregates, elements, and bases—are not established as real.
What is the investigation into the designation of intrinsic nature?

It refers to investigating within the correspondence between the designator and the designated among all phenomena that their intrinsic nature is merely the causal basis for the provisional designation of names and expressions.
What is the investigation into the designation of distinctions?

It refers to seeking out distinctions within the correspondence between the designators and the designated among all phenomena, [concluding that] these are merely the causal nature for the provisional establishment of conventional names and expressions.
Having correctly and diligently cultivated the investigation of phenomena (*dharmaparyeṣaṇā*), how does one give rise to knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtajñāna*) regarding phenomena?
It refers to the arising of four kinds of knowledge of things as they truly are:

first, the knowledge of things as they truly are induced by the investigation of names (*nāmaparyeṣaṇā*); second, the knowledge of things as they truly are induced by the investigation of things (*vastuparyeṣaṇā*); third, the knowledge of things as they truly are induced by the investigation of the designation of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaprajñaptiparyeṣaṇā*); and fourth, the knowledge of things as they truly are induced by the investigation of the designation of distinctions (*viśeṣaprajñaptiparyeṣaṇā*).
What is the knowledge of reality as it is, induced by the investigation of names?
It is the knowledge that, as it truly is, names are unapprehendable.
What is the knowledge of reality as it is, induced by the investigation of things?
It refers to the wisdom that knows, as they truly are, that even the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-nimitta*) are unapprehendable.
What is the wisdom that knows things as they truly are, which is induced by the thorough investigation of the provisional designation of intrinsic nature?
It refers to the wisdom that knows, as they truly are, that a substantially existent intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is unapprehendable.
What is the knowledge of reality as it is (yathābhūta-jñāna) induced by the investigation into the provisional designation of distinctions?
It refers to the knowledge that, when seeking distinctions in what truly exists, no such distinctions can be found.
For one who diligently cultivates samādhi in reliance upon the Dharma, how should the stages of yoga (yogabhūmi) be understood?
There are five kinds:
first, support; second, activity; third, mirror; fourth, illumination; and fifth, basis.
What is support?

This refers to the extensive learning regarding the levels of "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, as well as the noble truths, which has already been accumulated as the provisions for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*).
How is this practiced?
It is by means of appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) directed toward these objects.
What is the mirror?
It refers to the samādhi characterized by signs that takes objects as its condition.
What is the light?
This refers to the wisdom that realizes the non-apprehension of both the grasper and the grasped.
Based on this principle, the Buddha, the Blessed One, excellently proclaimed:
"When a bodhisattva is in the state of meditative equipoise, They observe that the reflected image is nothing but mind."
Once the conceptualization of objects has been eliminated, one scrutinizes that there is only the conceptualization of self.
Abiding thus within the internal mind, one knows that the apprehended object does not exist;
subsequently, the apprehending subject is also absent, until finally one touches the state of non-apprehension.
What is the basis? It is the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*),
because one abandons all heavy burdens (*dausthulya*) and attains the purified transformation of the basis.
Regarding all phenomena, what is skillfulness in phenomena?
It is due to extensive learning.
What is skillfulness in meaning?
This means that one thoroughly understands the characteristics within the Abhidharma and Vinaya.
What is skillfulness regarding the phrasing?
It means that one thoroughly understands the etymological explanations of words and phrases.
What is skill in terminology?
It refers to being able to thoroughly understand conventional expressions such as "self" and "mine," and speaking in accordance with them without deep attachment.
What is skill in the intentional meaning regarding the past and the future?
This means being able to skillfully understand the experience of the past limit (*pūrvānta*) and the transcendence from the future limit (*aparānta*).
Regarding how one dwells in the Dharma among all phenomena:

if one does not attain the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), but merely exerts oneself in the application of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī*), this is not called dwelling in the Dharma.
If one does not obtain hearing and reflection, but merely applies oneself diligently to the cultivation of wisdom through practice, this is also not called "abiding in the Dharma.
Only when one abides securely by attaining both types of skillful means is it called "abiding in the Dharma."
If one merely upholds, recites, and explains the Dharma to others, and contemplates its meaning, this is called the wisdom of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī prajñā*).
If one practices the means of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) without being satisfied, this is called the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī prajñā*).
The skillful means of samādhi refers to the skillful means of uninterrupted and earnest application, as well as the skillful means of non-erroneous application.
"Lack of contentment" refers to not giving rise to attachment while practicing the superior skillful means of śamatha.
For what reason is only one portion of the Vaipulya called the Bodhisattva-pāramitā-piṭaka?

Because within this portion all the pāramitās are explained extensively by way of their number, their characteristics, their sequence, their etymologies, their cultivation, their distinctions, their inclusion, their opposites, their qualities, and their mutual determination.
For what reason are the Vaipulya sections called "vast and profound"?
It is because the nature of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is vast and profound.
For what cause and condition do some sentient beings fail to give rise to resolute belief (*adhimukti*) in the vastness and profundity of the Vaipulya sections, but instead harbor fear?
Because they have distanced themselves from the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), because they have not planted roots of virtue, and because they are under the influence of evil friends.
For what reason and by what conditions do some beings, despite generating resolute belief (*adhimukti*) toward the vast and profound portions of the Vaipulya, fail to attain deliverance?
Because they dwell deeply in their own adherence to views and constantly and firmly cling to the literal meaning of words,
it was with this underlying intention that the Blessed One spoke these words in the *Mahādharmanirhāra-sūtra*:
"If bodhisattvas grasp at the meaning according to the words and do not investigate phenomena through correct reasoning, twenty-eight types of incorrect views will arise."

What are called the twenty-eight types of incorrect views? They are: the view of signs; the view of the deprecation of designations; the view of the deprecation of conceptualization; the view of the deprecation of reality; the view of grasping; the view of transformation;

the view of innocence; the view of renunciation; the view of contempt; the view of provocation; the view of inversion; the view of production; the view of not establishing a thesis; the view of equivocation; the view of service; the view of stubborn ignorance; the fundamental view; the view of seeing non-existence in what is seen; the view of abandoning skillful means; the view of non-renunciation; the view of obstructing increase; the view of producing non-merit; the view of no fruit for effort; the view of receiving humiliation; the view of slander; the view of being unfit for discourse; the view of vastness; and the view of overweening pride.
As it is said in the Vaipulya section:
"All phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature.
With what underlying intention was this said?
This means that because there is no nature of spontaneity, no nature of intrinsic substance, no abiding in intrinsic substance, and no nature of characteristics as apprehended by the foolish.
Furthermore, with respect to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), it is due to the absence of nature in terms of characteristics;
with respect to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), it is due to the absence of nature in terms of arising.
Regarding the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), it is because it is non-existent in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*).
Furthermore, concerning that, it is said:
"All phenomena are without arising and without cessation; they are quiescent from the beginning and parinirvāṇa by their very nature."
With what underlying intention was this said?
Just as there is no intrinsic nature, so too is there no arising.
Just as there is no arising, so too is there no cessation.
As there is no arising and no cessation, so too is primordial tranquility.
As there is primordial tranquility, so too is natural nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of intentions; by means of these intentions, all the intentions of the Tathāgatas within the Vaipulya section should be understood and resolved accordingly.
What are the four?

First, the intentionality of equality; second, the intentionality of another time; third, the intentionality of another meaning; and fourth, the intentionality regarding the inclinations of individuals.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of secrets; by means of these secrets, all the secrets of the Tathāgatas within the Vaipulya section should be correctly understood and resolved.
What are the four? First, the secret of entry; second, the secret of characteristics; third, the secret of antidotes; and fourth, the secret of transformation.
Furthermore, within the Vaipulya section, how can the characteristics of a bodhisattva who is skilled in the samādhi of phenomena be known?

It is said that this is due to five causes: first, the moment-to-moment elimination of the basis for all coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*); second, the emergence from various conceptualizations to experience the joy of the Dharma; third, the thorough knowledge of immeasurable non-conceptual characteristics; fourth, the constant presence of non-conceptual characteristics conducive to the side of purification; and fifth, the ability to sustain the causes for the complete accomplishment of the Buddha-body, which becomes increasingly superior and excellent.

The Dharma of the Śrāvaka-piṭaka and the Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka both flow from the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata; for what reason, then, does making offerings and showing reverence to the Bodhisattva-piṭaka with incense, garlands, and the like produce a vast and boundless accumulation of merit, whereas this is not the case for the Śrāvaka-piṭaka?

Because the Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka is the locus upon which the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings depend; because it is capable of establishing great purpose; and because it is the source from which the unsurpassed and immeasurable mass of great merit arises.
Chapter 3: On Attainment (Prāpti), Part One. What is the determination of attainment?
Briefly stated, there are two kinds:
first, for the purpose of establishing the person (pudgala); second, for the purpose of establishing clear realization (abhisamaya).
How are individuals (pudgala) established?

Briefly, there are seven types: namely, by way of the distinction of afflicted conduct, the distinction of renunciation, the distinction of sustenance, the distinction of skillful means, the distinction of fruition, the distinction of realm, and the distinction of practice; it should be understood that individuals are established in this manner.
What is the distinction of temperaments?

There are seven types, namely: the distinctions among individuals (pudgala) who are dominated by attachment, those dominated by aversion, those dominated by delusion, those dominated by pride, those dominated by discursive thought, those with balanced temperaments, and those with attenuated defilements.
What is the distinction of renunciation?
There are three kinds, namely, the distinction between individuals (pudgala) of the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Mahāyāna.
What is the distinction of maintenance?

There are three types: namely, the distinction between individuals who have not yet accumulated the provisions, those who have both accumulated and not yet accumulated the provisions, and those who have already accumulated the provisions.
What is the distinction of the means?
There are two kinds, namely, the distinction between the individuals who follow by faith and those who follow by dharma.
What is the distinction of the fruits?

There are twenty-seven types of these, namely: those with faith, those with resolute confidence, those who have attained vision, those who have realized through the body, those liberated by wisdom, those liberated both ways, those entering the stream, those established in the fruit of stream-entry, those entering the fruit of once-returning, those established in the fruit of once-returning, those entering the fruit of non-returning, those established in the fruit of non-returning, those entering the fruit of arhatship, and those established in the fruit of arhatship.

This is due to the distinctions among individuals (*pudgala*), namely: those who are reborn seven times at most (*saptakṛtvabhavaparama*), those who go from family to family (*kulaṃkula*), those with only one interval remaining (*ekavicika*), those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), those who attain parinirvāṇa upon being born (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), those who attain parinirvāṇa without exertion (*anabhisamskāraparinirvāyin*), those who attain parinirvāṇa with exertion (*sābhisamskāraparinirvāyin*), those who ascend to the higher realms (*ūrdhvasrotas*), Arhats subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*), Arhats intent on reflection (*cetana-dharman*), Arhats intent on guarding (*anurakṣaṇādharman*), Arhats abiding in the immovable (*sthitākampya*), Arhats capable of attaining the immovable (*prativedhanādharman*), and Arhats of the immovable nature (*akopyadharman*).
What is the differentiation by realm?
It refers to ordinary beings, those in training, and those beyond training within the desire realm.
As there are these three types in the desire realm, so it is likewise in the form and formless realms.
Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas of the desire and form realms; there are also pratyekabuddhas of the desire realm and the inconceivable *pudgala*s of the Tathāgatas—due to these distinctions.
What is the distinction in their practice?

Briefly, there are five types: first, the bodhisattva practicing through resolute belief; second, the bodhisattva practicing through superior intention; third, the bodhisattva practicing with signs; fourth, the bodhisattva practicing without signs; and fifth, the bodhisattva practicing without effort—these being the distinctions among individuals.
What is a person of greedy temperament?
It refers to one who possesses intense and long-lasting desire.
Likewise, persons of hateful, deluded, proud, and discursive temperaments all possess these same distinctions of intensity and duration.
What is a person of equal temperament (*sama-carita*)?
It refers to one whose afflictions abide in their natural state.
What is a person of slight passion (*manda-rajas-carita*)?
This refers to those whose afflictions are subtle and thin when abiding in their natural state.
What is a person belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle?
It refers to one who abides in the *dharmatā* of the Śrāvaka, whether of a determinate or indeterminate nature, and who is of dull faculties.

Seeking liberation for themselves, they give rise to vast and correct aspirations; cultivating the intention of renunciation and detachment from craving, they take the Śrāvaka Piṭaka as their object of focus, and through diligent practice of the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, they attain the end of suffering.

What is a person belonging to the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas? It refers to one who abides in the *dharmatā* of a Pratyekabuddha, whether of a determined or undetermined nature, and possesses middling faculties. Having personally sought liberation, they have formulated a vast and correct vow;

they cultivate the intention for renunciation and detachment from craving and the intention for the realization of awakening through personal effort. Taking the *Śrāvaka-piṭaka* as their object of focus, they diligently practice the "Dharma-conforming Dharma-practice" (*dharmānudharmapratipatti*). Whether they have previously not yet produced the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), or have previously produced them; whether they have previously not yet attained the fruits [of the path], or have previously attained them—they appear in a world devoid of a Buddha, where the Noble Path manifests solely through internal reflection.
Some dwell alone like the horn of a rhinoceros, while others attain the end of suffering through solitary or group practice.
What is a Mahāyāna *pudgala*?
It refers to one who abides in the *dharmatā* of a bodhisattva, whether of a concentrated or unconcentrated nature, and who possesses sharp faculties.

For the sake of seeking the liberation of all sentient beings, they generate vast and correct vows and cultivate the intention for non-abiding nirvana; taking the Bodhisattva-piṭaka as their objective sphere, they diligently practice the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, ripen sentient beings, purify Buddha-fields, receive the great prediction, and realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
What is a person who has not yet accumulated the provisions?

It refers to one who takes the superior dharma of the truths as their object, gives rise to a mild degree of pure faith and resolute conviction, and has accomplished a mild degree of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) that have not yet reached the stage of certainty regarding the time of rebirth.
What is a person who has already fulfilled or not yet fulfilled the provisions?

It refers to one who takes the Dharma predominant over the Truths as their object, gives rise to a middling degree of pure faith and resolute conviction, and has accomplished a middling degree of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) such that birth [in the next life] is certain.
What is the person who has already completed the provisions?

It refers to one who takes the Dharma predominant by means of the Truths as their object, gives rise to superior pure faith and resolute conviction, and accomplishes the superior factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) at this very birth.

Furthermore, one who has not yet completed the accumulations refers to one who takes the sublime Dharma conditioned by the Truths as their object, achieves the lowest degree of the patience for the discernment of phenomena (*dharmavicaya-kṣānti*) regarding those Truths, and achieves the lowest degree of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) at a time when birth [in the higher realms] is not yet certain.
Those who have already or have not yet fully accumulated the provisions (*sambhāra*) are as follows:

taking the Dharma that has the Truths as its sovereign object as their cognitive domain, they have achieved a medium degree of patient acceptance of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmanidhyānaksānti*) regarding the Truths, and have achieved a medium degree of the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) at the stage when birth is certain.

"One who has already completed the provisions" refers to one who takes the superior dharmas that have the truths as their object; such a person has achieved the highest degree of *dharmavicāra-kṣānti* (receptivity to the investigation of dharmas) regarding the truths and has achieved the highest degree of the *nirvedhabhāgīya* (aids to penetration) at the very moment of this birth.
Regarding the three grades of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) herein, these exclude the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).

This is because the nature of the Supreme Mundane Dharma consists of only a single moment and necessarily lacks continuity; thus, at the very moment it arises, one definitely enters the clear realization (*abhisamaya*), rather than remaining in a prior stage.

Regarding the lower and middle grades of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), there is the possibility of retrogression; however, this refers solely to the retrogression of active manifestations (*samudācāra*) and not to the retrogression of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), because those who have already produced roots of virtue based on *nirvāṇa* do not initiate them anew.
What is the person who follows by faith (śraddhānusārin)?
It refers to one who has already completed the provisions, whose nature is of dull faculties, and who cultivates the clear realization of the truths in accordance with the instruction of others.
What is a person who practices in accordance with the Dharma (dharmānusārī-pudgala)?

It refers to one who has already completed the accumulations, possesses a nature of sharp faculties, and spontaneously accords with the supreme Dharma of the Truths to cultivate the clear realization of the Truths (satyābhisamaya).
What is the person who is liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta)?
It refers to one who was previously a follower by faith (śraddhānusārin) and has now reached the stage of fruition.
What is the person who has attained through vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta)?
This refers to one who follows the Dharma (dharmānusārī) having already reached the stage of fruition.
What is a person who is a bodily witness (kāyasākṣin)?
It refers to those in training (śaikṣa) who have fully realized and attained the eight liberations (aṣṭavimokṣa).
What is a person liberated by wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta* pudgala)?
It refers to one who has exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*) but has not yet fully realized the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa-dhyāna*).
What is a person liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta* pudgala)?
This refers to those who have exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*) and have fully realized the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa-dhyāna*).
What is a person (*pudgala*) who is a candidate for the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-pratipannaka*)?
It refers to one who dwells in the stage of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), as well as one who dwells in the fifteen moments of mind of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
What is the person (pudgala) who has attained the fruit of stream-entry?
It refers to one abiding at the moment of the sixteenth mind-moment of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
This very path of seeing is also called "entering into the certainty of the right nature" (*samyaktvaniyāmāvakrānti*) and is also called "the clear realization of the dharma" (*dharmābhisamaya*).
If one who has not yet abandoned desire for the realm of desire subsequently enters the state of determination in rightness, they attain the fruit of stream-entry.
If one who has partially abandoned desire for the realm of desire subsequently enters the state of determination in rightness, they attain the fruit of once-returning.
If one who has already become detached from the desires of the desire realm subsequently enters the stage of the determination of rightness and attains the fruit of non-returning,

and if one who has already permanently severed all afflictions to be abandoned by the path of seeing attains the fruit of stream-entry— why then is it said that one attains the fruit of stream-entry only by permanently severing the three fetters?
Because it is the most supreme [of obstacles]. Why is it the most supreme?
Because it is a cause for not setting out toward liberation; and even if one has already set out, it is a cause for a false departure as well as a cause for an improper departure.
Furthermore, these three fetters are the causes for delusion regarding the objects of knowledge, the causes for delusion regarding views, and the causes for delusion regarding the antidotes.
What is a person who is a candidate for the fruit of Once-returner?
This refers to one who, within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), has already abandoned the five grades of afflictions of the desire realm and abides in that path.
What is a person (*pudgala*) who is a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*)?
This refers to one who, within the path of cultivation, has already abandoned the sixth grade of afflictions of the desire realm and abides in that path.
What is the person who is a candidate for the stage of non-returner?
It refers to one who, within the path of cultivation, has already abandoned the seventh and eighth grades of afflictions of the desire realm and abides in that path.
What is a person (pudgala) who has attained the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala)?
It refers to one who, within the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), has already abandoned the ninth grade of afflictions of the desire realm and abides in that path.

If one has already permanently abandoned all afflictions to be abandoned by the path of seeing (darśanamārga), as well as all afflictions of the desire realm to be abandoned by the path of cultivation, thereby attaining the fruit of non-returning, for what reason is it said only that one attains the fruit of non-returning by permanently abandoning the five lower fetters (pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni)?
Because it is the most excellent inclusion.
Why is it the most excellent?
Because it serves as the superior cause for the lower realms and the lower destinies.
What is the person who is a candidate for arhatship?
It refers to one who has already permanently abandoned the eight categories of afflictions of the Peak of Existence and abides in that path.
What is the person who has attained the fruit of arhatship?
This refers to one who has already permanently abandoned the ninth grade of afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and abides in that ultimate path.

If an Arhat has permanently abandoned all afflictions of the three realms, why is it said only that by permanently abandoning the five higher fetters (*pañca ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*), one attains the fruit of Arhatship?
Because it is the most excellent inclusion.
Why is it the most excellent?
Because it is both the cause for taking up the higher realms and the cause for not abandoning the higher realms.
What is the person who is "at most seven times reborn"?
This refers to one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry and, through alternating births among humans and gods, undergoes rebirth for at most seven times before reaching the end of suffering.
What is a person who goes from family to family (*kulaṃkula*)?
It refers to one who, having attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), reaches the end of suffering after passing from family to family, whether among the gods or among human beings.
What is the person who is an ekabijin (one-seeded)?
It refers to one who is a sakṛdāgāmin (once-returner), or one who, having been reborn in the heavenly realms, attains the end of suffering after undergoing only one more existence.
What is the person who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state?
This refers to one for whom the fetters of birth have already been abandoned, but the fetters of arising have not yet been abandoned;

such a person either attains the end of suffering as soon as the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) arises and the Noble Path manifests, or, having already arisen in the intermediate state in order to proceed toward the existence of birth (*upapattibhava*), attains the end of suffering as soon as the thought of proceeding arises and the Noble Path manifests.
Or, having reflected and set out toward birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*), before reaching that birth-existence, the Noble Path manifests and one attains the end of suffering.
What is the person who attains parinirvāṇa upon birth (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*)?
This refers to one for whom both fetters are as yet unbroken, who, immediately upon being born in the form realm, brings the noble path into manifestation and attains the end of suffering.
What is "attaining parinirvāṇa without exertion"?
That is to say, having been born there, one realizes the path of the noble ones without further application of effort and thus attains the end of suffering.
What kind of person is one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion?
This means that having been born there, through the power of application (*prayoga*), the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) manifests, whereby one attains the end of suffering.
What is the person who goes upward (*ūrdhvasrotas*)?

It refers to one who, having taken birth in each successive stage (*bhūmi*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), finally enters the Akaniṣṭha heaven, where the untainted Noble Path manifests, and thereby attains the end of suffering.
Furthermore, there are those who proceed as far as the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), where the Noble Path manifests and they attain the end of suffering.
Moreover, there are five grades of distinction in the mixed cultivation (*vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā*) of the fourth dhyāna:
first, inferior cultivation; second, middling cultivation; third, superior cultivation; fourth, superior-excellent cultivation; and fifth, supreme cultivation.
By means of this fivefold mixed cultivation of the fourth dhyāna, one is born in the five Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa) respectively.
What is a *parihāṇadharman* arhat?

It refers to one of dull faculties who, whether distracted or undistracted, whether reflecting or not reflecting, may fall away from the blissful dwelling in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
What is the arhat who must contemplate the dharma?

This refers to one of dull faculties who, whether distracted or undistracted, may fall away from the dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*) if they do not contemplate, but who is able to avoid such falling away once they have contemplated.
What is the Arhat who protects the Dharma?
This refers to one of dull faculties whose meditative dwelling in happiness in the present life may be lost if he becomes distracted, yet remains undisturbed if he does not become distracted.
What is the Arhat who dwells in immovability?
It refers to one of dull faculties who, whether distracted or undistracted, is able to never fall away from the dwelling in happiness in the present life, yet is unable to refine their faculties.
What is the *prativedhanā-dharman* arhat?

This refers to one of dull faculties who, whether distracted or undistracted, is able to never fall away from the dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*), yet is capable of refining their faculties (*indriyasaṃcāra*).
What is the Arhat of immovable dharma?
It refers to one of sharp faculties who, whether distracted or undistracted, is capable of not falling away from the dwelling in happiness in the present life.
What is a person who is an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) in the desire realm?
It refers to one who is born or has grown up in the desire realm and has not attained the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*).
What is a person who is a learner (*śaikṣa*) in the desire realm?
This refers to those born or raised in the desire realm who have already attained the noble dharmas but still possess residual fetters.
What is a person (pudgala) in the desire realm who is beyond training (aśaikṣa)?
This refers to those born or raised in the desire realm who have already attained the noble dharmas and possess no further fetters.
As there are three such cases in the desire realm, so it is likewise in the form and formless realms.
What is a bodhisattva-pudgala of the desire or form realms?
It refers to one who, possessing the characteristics of having abandoned birth in the formless realms and being established in the bliss of dhyāna, is born in the desire realm or the form realm.
What is a person who is a pratyekabuddha in the desire realm?
It refers to one who, when no Buddha has appeared in the world, is born in the desire realm and spontaneously realizes the awakening of a pratyekabuddha.
What is the inconceivable person (pudgala) that is the Tathāgata?

It refers, first of all, to his manifestation within the desire realm, beginning from his dwelling in the wondrous jewel palace of Tuṣita Heaven, up until his manifestation of the Great Parinirvāṇa, manifesting all the great practices performed by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
What is a bodhisattva individual who practices through resolute belief?
It refers to one who dwells on the stage of practice through resolute belief and has accomplished the lower, middle, and superior levels of patience.
What is a bodhisattva individual who practices through the higher resolve?
This refers to all bodhisattvas within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
What is a bodhisattva *pudgala* who practices with signs?

It refers to all bodhisattvas dwelling in the stages of the Utmost Joy (*pramuditā*), the Stainless (*vimalā*), the Luminous (*prabhākārī*), the Radiant Wisdom (*arciṣmatī*), the Extremely Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā*), and the Manifest (*abhimukhī*).
What is a bodhisattva person who practices the signless?
It refers to all bodhisattvas dwelling in the stage of Far-Going (dūramgamā-bhūmi).
What is a bodhisattva person who practices without effort (anābhoga)?
This refers to all bodhisattvas dwelling in the stages of Immovable, Good Intelligence, and Cloud of Dharma.
Furthermore, as it is said regarding the person (pudgala) who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna), there are two types:
first, those who attain liberation gradually; second, those who attain liberation instantaneously.
Regarding gradual transcendence, it has been explained extensively as before.

Regarding instantaneous transcendence, this refers to having entered the clear realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*), relying upon the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) to produce a supramundane path that instantaneously severs all afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms.
The distinct severance of each category establishes only two fruits: namely, the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) and the fruit of arhatship (*arhat-phala*).
Such a person-gone (*pudgala*) mostly discerns the noble intent either in the present life or at the time of death;

even if they cannot so discern it, by the power of their aspiration, they are reborn in the desire realm through that very power of aspiration and, having emerged in a world without a Buddha, they achieve the fruit of a solitary victor (*pratyekabuddha*).
